interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: McCollum v. Sieben, 211 F.2d 708 (8th Cir. 1954)
interps.summary: The court applied the federal beneficiary-designation rule governing National Service Life Insurance proceeds, holding that the named beneficiary’s entitlement was not altered by a state divorce decree or property settlement. Federal law therefore preempted any contrary state-law allocation of the insurance proceeds.
excerpts: Neither in the property settlement nor in the divorce proceedings is any reference made to the insurance policies here involved. No act or expression of the insured is even referred to in the evidence indicating that the insured desired or ever intended to change the named beneficiary. Wissner v. Wissner, 338 U.S. 655, 658, 70 S.Ct. 398, 400, 94 L.Ed. 424, is a case in which a soldier named his mother beneficiary in his National Life Insurance policy.

The controlling section of the Act provides that the insured ‘shall have the right to designate the beneficiary or beneficiaries of the insurance (within a designated class), * * * and shail * * * at all times have the right to change the beneficiary or beneficiaries * * *.’ 38 U.S.C. § 802(g), 38 U.S. C.A. § 802(g). Thus Congress has spoken with force and clarity in directing that the proceeds belong to the named beneficiary and no othe

norms.b_justification: McCollum interpreted 38 U.S.C. § 802(g), which gave the insured the exclusive federal-law right to designate and change the beneficiary of National Service Life Insurance. Its refusal to recognize a contrary state-law allocation is functionally consistent with the current federal-preemption rule protecting federally established rights and preventing state-law frustration of federal objectives; the current text is unavailable, so verbatim identity cannot be established.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Quivey, 292 F.2d 252 (8th Cir. 1961)
interps.summary: The court held that a widow’s allowance paid under Nebraska’s descent statutes was a terminable interest because it was payable from estate assets in which interests could pass to persons other than the surviving spouse. It therefore did not qualify for the estate-tax marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a).
excerpts: Subsection (a) of § 2056 of the 1954 Code provides for a marital deduction from the value of a decedent’s gross estate, of “an amount equal to the value of any interest in property which passes or has passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse”, subject to the limitations contained in subsections (b), (c), and (d).

A widow’s allowance under the Nebraska statutes, payable as it is out of assets of the estate not bequeathed or otherwise descending to her, must, we think, be held to constitute a terminable interest within these provisions of the Code and the Treasury Regulations, and so not to qualify as a marital deduction under § 2056(a) of the Code.

norms.b_justification: United States v. Quivey interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a) and the terminable-interest limitation in § 2056(b)(1)(A). The relevant language—an interest in property passing from the decedent to the surviving spouse and the limitation where an interest passes to another person—remains substantively unchanged in the current text; later amendments affected other provisions or subsection references, not these interpreted clauses.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Estate of Peyton v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, 323 F.2d 438 (8th Cir. 1963)
interps.summary: The court addressed whether the residue of the decedent’s estate qualified for the federal estate-tax marital deduction under § 2056. It applied the terminable-interest limitation in § 2056(b)(1) to the widow’s interest.
excerpts: This estate tax petition for review concerns the qualification of an estate’s residue for the marital deduction under § 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. The Tax Court, in an opinion not reviewed by the full court and not officially reported, resolved the issue against the estate.
On July 3 the Commissioner ruled that the residue did not qualify for the marital deduction because he regarded the interest as terminable within the meaning of § 2056(b) (1)

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(1), particularly the terminable-interest limitation on the marital deduction. The listed post-decision amendments do not amend § 2056(b)(1), so the provision’s relevant wording and function remain identical to those applied in Estate of Peyton; the method is functional-review because no verbatim quotation of the interpreted language appears in the excerpts.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bookwalter v. Lamar, 323 F.2d 664 (8th Cir. 1963)
interps.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction limitation for life estates and other terminable interests under § 2056(b)(1). It held that the widow’s interest vested absolutely upon the decedent’s death and was not disqualified by the will’s contingent gift-over provisions.
excerpts: The basic issue in this case is whether Maude H. Lamar (appellee), widow of Frederick C. Lamar, deceased, is entitled to the “marital deduction” of 50% of the value of the adjusted gross estate of Mr. Lamar under the provisions of § 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. More precisely, was the interest in the estate devised to the widow by decedent in his last will and testament a terminable one within the meaning of the statute, so as to disqualify her from claiming the “marital deduction,” — as contended by the Director, or, did the devised property vest absolutely in the widow immediately upon Lamar’s death, free of any contingency — as urged by appellee and as found by the trial court

Section 2056 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, the statutory authority for the “marital deduction,” also provides for a limitation in the case of a life estate or other terminable interest. Pertinent hereto is that portion of the limitation which reads: “(b) Limitation in the case of life estate or other terminable interest.— “(1) General rule. — Where, on the lapse of time, on the occurrence of an event or contingency, or on the failure of an event or contingency to occur, an interest passing to the surviving spouse will terminate or fail, no deduction shall be allowed under this section with respect to such interest- — • “(A) if an interest in such property passes or has passed (for less than an adequate and full consideration in money or money’s worth) from the decedent to any person other than such surviving spouse (or the estate of such spouse); and “(B) if by reason of such passing such person (or his heirs or assigns) may possess or enjoy any part of such property after such

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(1)(A)–(B), concerning terminable interests and interests passing to persons other than the surviving spouse. The quoted statutory language appears verbatim in the current text, and the listed post-decision amendments do not alter these subparagraphs.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bookwalter v. Phelps, 325 F.2d 186 (8th Cir. 1963)
interps.summary: The court applied the federal estate-tax marital-deduction rules to determine whether a Missouri probate-court widow’s allowance was a terminable interest under § 2056(b)(1). It held that the lump-sum allowance, which became the surviving spouse’s property, qualified for the marital deduction.
excerpts: The issue presented by this appeal is whether the widow’s allowance made by the probate court to the surviving spouse under Missouri law in the form of a lump sum award of $20,000, which in fact has been paid to the surviving spouse, qualifies for the marital deduction under § 2056 I.R.C.1954. More specifically, the issue is whether the Missouri widow’s allowance here involved is a terminable interest and hence not subject to the marital deduction.
Judge Oliver, in a memorandum opinion reported at 210 F.Supp. 801, rejects the Government’s contention that the Missouri widow’s allowance here involved Is a terminable interest.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(1), particularly the terminable-interest limitation as applied to a Missouri widow’s allowance. The amendment history identifies no post-1963 amendment to subsection (b)(1), and the current text retains the same terminable-interest rule in wording and function; the excerpts do not quote the statutory language verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Prudential Insurance Co. of America v. King, 453 F.2d 925 (8th Cir. 1971)
interps.summary: The court held that Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance is governed by the federal statutory scheme, which preempts contrary state law concerning the insurance and beneficiary designation. It therefore treated the dispute as controlled by the federal acts rather than state community-property or family-law rules.
excerpts: It is the contention of the plaintiff, in part at least, that the state law governs while the defendant contends that the decision rests solely on the federal acts of Congress. Title 38 U.S.C.A. ss. 765 to 776. We think that Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance is a contract between the United States government and approved insurers for the benefit of the insureds, the same being those entering the military service of the United States. The designation of insurers by the federal government under regulations prescribed by the federal act amounts to a preemption of the field of servicemen’s life insurance and it is therefore subject to the rules and regulations provided in the federal acts.

norms.b_justification: Prudential interpreted 38 U.S.C.A. §§ 765–776, including § 770(a), and held that federal Servicemen’s Group Life Insurance law preempted contrary state-law rules. That application is functionally consistent with the current federal-preemption rule protecting federal benefits programs from conflicting state family-property or domestic-relations laws, although the quoted language does not appear verbatim in the current text.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Burke v. United States, 459 F.2d 1017 (8th Cir. 1972)
interps.summary: The court applied the federal beneficiary-designation rules governing war risk insurance and held that the insured serviceman’s designation controlled. The federal scheme displaced the appellant’s contrary claim based on state family or community-property principles.
excerpts: Similarly, we find no unjust enrichment or “windfall” to the appellee. A review of the history of war risk insurance discloses that during wartime Congress closely circumscribed the class of permissible beneficiaries to insure that proceeds of such policies would go to persons dependent upon the insured soldier for financial support. Congress in 1946, however, broadened the Act by granting insured servicemen the right to designate their choice of beneficiaries and with the right at all times to change such designations without the consent of the beneficiaries.

Pursuant to such congressional command, the appellee contracted to pay the policy proceeds to Burke’s choice. Unfortunately for the appellant, Burke chose his father and brother. See Wissner v. Wissner, 338 U.S. 655, 658, 70 S.Ct. 398, 94 L.Ed. 424 (1950).

norms.b_justification: Burke interpreted 38 U.S.C. § 717(a) and held that the federal beneficiary-designation scheme controlled over contrary state-law claims to the insurance proceeds. Although the current text contains no verbatim quotation and the provision’s wording cannot be compared directly, Burke applies the same functional federal-preemption principle reflected in the current rule: federal benefits law protects federally established rights from conflicting state family-property law.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Landess v. Weinberger, 490 F.2d 1187 (8th Cir. 1974)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied the disabled-widow benefits provision in reviewing the Secretary’s denial of benefits. It held that the record did not adequately support the denial and remanded for further evidentiary proceedings.
excerpts: This is an appeal from the district court’s grant of summary judgment in favor of the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare on the basis that substantial evidence supported the Secretary’s denial for disabled widow’s insurance benefits under 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e) (1)(B)(ii) and 405(g). We reverse with directions to the district court to remand the case to the Secretary for further evidentiary proceedings.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(1)(B)(ii), requiring a disabled widow aged 50–59 to have a disability beginning before the end of the specified period. The 1983 amendment changed only the cross-reference from paragraph (5) to paragraph (4) as part of statutory renumbering, leaving the requirement identical in function to the current text.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Folkerds v. United States, 494 F.2d 749 (8th Cir. 1974)
interps.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction provision to determine whether property passing to the surviving spouse remained available for deduction after abatement for debts, expenses, and taxes. It held that Iowa’s abatement rules caused the relevant charges to reduce the daughter’s share rather than the widow’s share, permitting the claimed marital deduction.
excerpts: This is an action brought pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1) (1970) to recover $17,001.25 in federal estate taxes alleged to have been overpaid by the estate of A. C. Brocka. The facts are not in dispute. The controversy centers on whether, under Brocka’s will and Iowa law, certain property passing to the surviving spouse abates for the purpose of paying debts, costs of administration and federal estate taxes. If it does abate, there will be no marital deduction (since no corresponding interest passed to the surviving spouse), and the federal estate tax will be substantially increased.

The issue, then, relates to abatement; specifically, whether the debts, charges and federal estate tax are taken from the widow’s interest or that of the daughter. This is a matter to be determined by Iowa law. Riggs v. Del Drago, 317 U.S. 95, 63 S.Ct. 109, 87 L.Ed. 106 (1942).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the operative marital-deduction language in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a), concerning an interest in property that “passes or has passed” from the decedent to the surviving spouse. The later 1981 amendment only changed the cross-reference from “subsections (b) and (c)” to “subsection (b)” after former subsection (c) was repealed; it did not alter the wording or function of the provision governing whether the spouse received a deductible interest.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Williams v. Williams, 532 F.2d 120 (8th Cir. 1976)
interps.summary: The court applied Younger abstention and comity principles to bar declaratory and injunctive relief that would nullify a Missouri adoption decree. It emphasized that domestic relations are traditionally within the province of the states and that state collateral remedies had not been exhausted.
excerpts: The application for declaratory and injunctive relief is barred by the comity principles of Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37, 91 S.Ct. 746, 27 L.Ed.2d 669 (1971) and Huffmann v. Pursue, Ltd., 420 U.S. 592, 95 S.Ct. 1200, 43 L.Ed.2d 482 (1975). To grant the relief sought would nullify the decree of a Missouri court. This decree relates to an area, domestic relations, which has traditionally been the province of the states.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Mattis v. Schnarr, 547 F.2d 1007 (8th Cir. 1976)
interps.summary: The court treated the right to conceive and raise one's children as a fundamental liberty interest protected by due process. It considered that parental-rights interest in evaluating a challenge to Missouri’s deadly-force rules governing police pursuit of fleeing suspects.
excerpts: Among the rights that have been declared fundamental in due process analysis are the right to abort a pregnancy (encompassed within the right to privacy), Roe v. Wade, supra; to be free of restrictive maternity leave regulations that burden “the freedom of personal choice in matters of marriage and family life,” Cleveland Board of Education v. LaFleur, 414 U.S. 632, 639-640, 94 S.Ct. 791, 796, 39 L.Ed.2d 52 (1974); and the “rights to conceive and raise one’s children,” Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645, 651, 92 S.Ct. 1208, 1212, 31 L.Ed.2d 551 (1972).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: M. S. v. Wermers, 557 F.2d 170 (8th Cir. 1977)
interps.summary: The court recognized parents’ constitutionally protected authority to direct the care, custody, education, and upbringing of their minor children. It applied that principle to conclude that parents may be informed of and attempt to address a minor child’s litigation, consistent with preserving the family relationship.
excerpts: In addition to restriction by the state, minors are subject to parental custody and control. “Constitutional interpretation has consistently recognized that the parents’ claim to authority in their own household to direct the rearing of their children is basic to the structure of society. It is cardinal that the custody, care and nurture of the child reside first in the parents whose primary function and freedom include preparation for obligations the state can neither supply nor hinder.” Carey v. New York, -U.S.-,---, 97 S.Ct. 2010, 2028, 52 L.Ed.2d 675 (1977).

Judicial decisions have enveloped the sanctity of the family and parental authority with constitutional protection because the institution of the family has long been recognized as a cornerstone of our law. Moore v. East Cleveland,-U.S.-, 97 S.Ct. 1932, 52 L.Ed.2d 531 (1977); Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205, 92 S.Ct. 1526, 32 L.Ed.2d 15 (1972); Ginsberg v. New York, supra; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 45 S.Ct. 571, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Overman v. United States, 563 F.2d 1287 (8th Cir. 1977)
interps.summary: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 659 waived sovereign immunity only for state garnishment proceedings enforcing child-support or alimony obligations, and did not authorize a broader damages or validity challenge against the United States or its disbursing officer. It further reasoned that § 660's expressly certified jurisdictional mechanism did not extend to § 659 actions, and remanded the remaining domestic-relations dispute to state court under the federal policy against federal adjudication of such matters.
excerpts: In 42 U.S.C. § 659 (Supp.1975), the United States waived its immunity from state garnishment actions directed at federal employees. The statute simply removed the bar of sovereign immunity to one narrow class of actions: enforcement of garnishment writs issued by state courts. See, e. g., Wilhelm v. United States Department of Air Force Accounting, 418 F.Supp. 162, 164 (S.D.Tex.1976). Nothing in the statute or legislative history, however, indicates any congressional intent to expose the Government to wider liability.

Congressman Ullman’s comment about certification is a reference to 42 U.S.C. § 660 (Supp. 1975). That provision provides federal jurisdiction for civil actions arising under 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(8) (Supp. 1975), if certified by the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare. Since §§ 652(a)(8) and 659 are parallel provisions, that is, both are part of Pub.L. 93-647, § 606(a), 88 Stat. 2351, 2357, the presumption must be that if Congress had intended federal jurisdiction for cases arising under § 659 it would have explicitly provided for it, as it did for § 652(a)(8).

norms.b_justification: Overman interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 660’s grant of federal jurisdiction for civil actions arising under § 652(a)(8) when certified by the Secretary, and the current text retains that same jurisdictional mechanism and venue provisions. The 1984 amendment only changed the agency name from Health, Education, and Welfare to Health and Human Services, a technical change that does not alter the provision’s wording in substance or function.

provisions: 42 U.S.C. § 660 (jurisdiction for actions arising under 42 U.S.C. § 652(a)(8), upon certification)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Stivers v. Minnesota, 575 F.2d 200 (8th Cir. 1978)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit affirmed dismissal under Younger abstention and related principles of federalism and comity. It held that abstention was not defeated merely because the federal plaintiffs were not named parties in the ongoing state family-law proceedings or because they claimed state remedies had been exhausted.
excerpts: As we read their brief, appellants, who are appealing pro se, contend that the three-judge district court erred in applying Younger principles to them because they were not named parties in the state court action. They also argue that state court remedies have been exhausted and that the principles of comity and federalism no longer apply. We reject both arguments and affirm.

The dismissal was grounded on the principles of federalism and comity set forth by the Supreme Court in Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37, 91 5. Ct. 746, 27 L.Ed.2d 669 (1971); Samuels v. Mackell, 401 U.S. 66, 91 S.Ct. 764, 27 L.Ed.2d 688 (1971); and Huffman v. Pursue, Ltd., 420 U.S. 592, 95 S.Ct. 1200, 43 L.Ed.2d 482 (1975). Stivers and Cherry appeal the order of dismissal.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Syrovatka v. Erlich, 608 F.2d 307 (8th Cir. 1979)
interps.summary: The court held that a parent’s presence at a termination hearing does not, by itself, establish constitutionally adequate notice. Applying procedural due process principles, it required notice stating the hearing’s date, time, and place, the proceeding’s purpose and possible consequences, the factual basis for the proposed commitment, and the governing legal standard.
excerpts: A finding that the parents were present at the hearing does not necessarily mean that the notice complied with procedural due process. The procedural due process requirements for parental rights termination hearings were announced in Alsager v. District Court of Polk County, 406 F.Supp. 10, 24-25 (S.D. Iowa 1975), aff’d, 545 F.2d 1137 (8th Cir. 1976). The notice requirements outlined in In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1, 87 S.Ct. 1428, 18 L.Ed.2d 527 (1967) were applied to parental termination hearings in Alsager.

notice should include the date, time and place of the hearing; a clear statement of the purpose of the proceedings and the possible consequences to the subject thereof; the alleged factual basis for the proposed commitment; and a statement of the legal standard upon which commitment is authorized.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bailey v. Califano, 614 F.2d 146 (8th Cir. 1980)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 402(e) in determining entitlement to disabled widow’s benefits. It held that the claimant satisfied the statutory disability requirements and was entitled to benefits.
excerpts: Ruby Darlene Bailey, a sixty-two-year-old widow, appeals from a district court judgment affirming a finding by the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare that she was ineligible for disabled widow’s benefits under 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e) and 423(d)(2)(B). We hold that Mrs. Bailey is entitled to benefits and reverse.

There is no dispute as to the applicable statutes and regulations. To be entitled to benefits, a widow has the burden of proving that her physical and mental impairments “are of a level of severity which under regulations prescribed by the Secretary is deemed to be sufficient to preclude an individual from engaging in any gainful activity.” 42 U.S.C. § 423(d)(2)(B).

norms.b_justification: Bailey interpreted the disabled-widow eligibility standard incorporated through 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(1)(B)(ii) and the referenced disability definition in § 423(d)(2)(B). The current text preserves that standard; later amendments to § 402(e) changed surrounding eligibility provisions and renumbered cross-references, but did not substantively alter the disability requirement at issue.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bergstrom v. Bergstrom, 623 F.2d 517 (8th Cir. 1980)
interps.summary: The court applied the domestic-relations exception to require dismissal of a federal custody dispute where resolving the constitutional claim would require factual reexamination and possible modification of the state custody arrangement. It held that the custody issue belonged exclusively in state court, particularly while related state proceedings were pending.
excerpts: Where a constitutional issue arises out of a custody dispute, and the initial determination involves a reexamination of the custody arrangement, the proper course is to dismiss the case and remand to the state court.

Since the primary issue is whether changed circumstances warrant modification of the custody arrangement, the constitutional question was obviously not presented in the posture of strict necessity. Under the circumstances, the district court should have declined to exercise jurisdiction.

Reexamination of custody arrangements is a matter which belongs exclusively in state court; domestic relations disputes have been traditionally subject to exclusive state jurisdiction. See Popovici v. Agler, 280 U.S. 379, 50 S.Ct. 154, 74 L.Ed. 489 (1930); Overman v. United States, 563 F.2d 1287, 1290 (8th Cir. 1977).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Navedo v. Preisser, 630 F.2d 636 (8th Cir. 1980)
interps.summary: The court applied intermediate scrutiny to Iowa’s gender-based statutory-rape classification under the Equal Protection Clause. It held that the State had not shown that limiting liability to male defendants and female victims was substantially related to important objectives such as preventing pregnancy or emotional harm.
excerpts: Gender-based classifications are subject to scrutiny under the equal protection clause, Reed v. Reed, 404 U.S. 71, 75, 92 S.Ct. 251, 253, 30 L.Ed.2d 225 (1971), including those classifications which discriminate against men. Orr v. Orr, 440 U.S. 268, 279, 99 S.Ct. 1102, 1111, 59 L.Ed.2d 306 (1979).

The state contends that the statutory rape provisions of § 698.1 had, in essence, two objectives; protecting certain young, unmarried females from unwanted pregnancies and from the possibly traumatic emotional effects of sexual intercourse with an older man who may wield undue influence oyer her. Although the state has provided no actual evidence of the statute’s purpose, it seems apparent from the face of the statute that those were the objectives intended.

In this case, the general doubts expressed by the First Circuit regarding a pregnancy rationale are reinforced by the peculiar structure of the Iowa statute. That statute superimposes strict age limitations upon its gender distinction, thereby excluding from punishment the class of males most likely to have intercou
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Fulton v. Harris, 658 F.2d 641 (8th Cir. 1981)
interps.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s dependency rules, including the provision deeming a child dependent when the child could inherit from the insured parent under applicable state intestacy law. It relied on equal-protection precedent invalidating Arkansas’s discriminatory intestacy rule and concluded that the child’s eligibility could not be defeated by that unconstitutional nonmarital-status classification.
excerpts: In addressing appellant’s contention that her daughter is entitled to child’s insurance benefits, we note initially that under the statute a child is deemed dependent on the deceased wage earner unless the child is illegitimate and is not living with the insured parent or is not receiving support from that parent. 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(3)(A). A child is deemed legitimate and, consequently, dependent if she may inherit personal property from the insured parent under the law of the state where that parent was domiciled at the time of his death. Mathews v. Lucas, 427 U.S. 495, 514-15 n.17, 96 S.Ct. 2755, 2766-67 n.17, 49 L.Ed.2d 651 (1976); 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and the dependency provisions in 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1)(C)(ii) and § 402(d)(3)(A), including the state-law inheritance rule for determining legitimacy and dependency. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively amend those provisions; later changes elsewhere in § 416 are unrelated, so the interpreted rule remains identical in wording and function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Gross ex rel. Scott v. Harris, 664 F.2d 667 (8th Cir. 1981)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), which requires determining entitlement to child insurance benefits by referring to the law of the insured’s domicile governing intestate succession. It held that the former Missouri provisions conditioning an illegitimate child’s paternal inheritance—and thus eligibility for benefits—on the father’s marriage to the mother and recognition of the child were unconstitutional under the equal-protection principles applied in Trimble.
excerpts: 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) states: (2)(A) In determining whether an applicant is the child or parent of a fully or currently insured individual for purposes of this subchapter, the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which such insured individual is domiciled at the time such applicant files application, or, if such insured individual is dead, by the courts of the State in which he was domiciled at the time of his death, or, if such insured individual is or was not so domiciled in any State, by the courts of the District of Columbia.

Our inquiry, however, is not ended by a simple comparison of the statutes. In order to resolve this litigation, it remains for us to determine (1) whether the statute is unconstitutional in whole or only in part, and (2) whether the Trimble decision may be applied retrospectively so that the appellants may benefit from that decision. We shall address these issues seriatim.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Estate of McMillan v. Commissioner, 670 F.2d 788 (8th Cir. 1982)
interps.summary: The court applied the terminable-interest rule under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b) to determine whether the surviving spouse’s bequest qualified for the estate-tax marital deduction. It held that the will created a life estate without an unrestricted power to appoint the principal, so the relevant portion of the bequest did not qualify for the deduction.
excerpts: Appellant, Mary E. McMillan, challenges the Tax Court’s determination that a portion of a bequest to her under her late husband’s will did not qualify for the marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b) (1976). McMillan v. Commissioner, 76 T.C. No. 13, slip op. (Jan. 29, 1981). For the reasons set forth herein, we affirm.

After Mrs. McMillan filed an estate tax return claiming a marital deduction for one half of the property of the estate, $899,263, the Commissioner filed a notice of deficiency declaring that the marital deduction amounted to only $42,136. This decision was based on the Commissioner’s belief that the bequest to Mrs. McMillan was a life estate without a power of appointment over the principal. Under the terminable interest rule, as embodied in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b), such an interest is considered a terminable interest and does not qualify for the marital deduction.

norms.b_justification: The decision applied the terminable-interest rule in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b), concerning whether a surviving spouse’s life-estate bequest qualified for the marital deduction, including the absence of a power of appointment over principal. The post-decision amendments listed do not alter the relevant language or function of § 2056(b)(1) or the applicable life-estate/power-of-appointment provisions, so the rule remains functionally identical.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Paris v. Schweiker, 674 F.2d 707 (8th Cir. 1982)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(5) to determine eligibility for disabled widow’s benefits. It held that Mrs. Paris satisfied the age and widow-status requirements and was disabled within the meaning of the Act, requiring payment of the benefits.
excerpts: The test of disability for a widow claimant is more stringent than for a person claiming under wage earner status. A widow claimant must be at least fifty years old, be the widow of a wage earner who died fully insured, and have become disabled within seven years of the wage earner’s death. See 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(5). Here, there is no dispute that Mrs. Paris was fifty-seven years old at the time of the hearing and was the widow of Charles D. Paris, who died fully insured on March 8, 1979. The only issue is whether Mrs. Paris was disabled at the time of her claim.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the widow’s disability-duration requirement then codified at 42 U.S.C. § 402(e)(5), requiring disability to begin within seven years of the fully insured wage earner’s death. The 1983 amendment redesignated that provision as § 402(e)(4) and updated cross-references without substantively changing its language or function; the current text retains the same requirement through the reference to the “period specified in paragraph (4).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Derheim v. Hennepin County Welfare Board, 688 F.2d 66 (8th Cir. 1982)
interps.summary: The court rejected the substantive due process challenge to revocation of a foster-care license based on evidence of the foster parent’s juvenile assaultive offense. It held that the cited family-related substantive due process precedents did not limit the state’s authority and obligation to regulate foster children and those licensed to care for them.
excerpts: About all that can be said about these cases is that each established or vindicated an important substantive right under the Constitution, and all probably had something to do with the interests of a family unit as opposed to the state’s interests. They do not, however, individually or collectively, even arguably impose the limitation which the appellants suggest on the state’s power and obligation to deal with foster children and those whom it has licensed to care for them.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Yost v. Schweiker, 699 F.2d 438 (8th Cir. 1983)
interps.summary: The court applied rational-basis review under the equal-protection component of the Fifth Amendment to 42 U.S.C. § 402(7), which limits Social Security survivor benefits when a survivor is entitled to Railroad Retirement Act benefits. It held that the provision was constitutional despite denying benefits to the divorced surviving spouse because the deceased worker was insured under both systems.
excerpts: The sole issue presented in this appeal is whether section 202(7) of the Social Security Act, which limits the benefits that survivors of individuals who are fully insured under both the Social Security Act and the Railroad Retirement Act may receive, violates the equal protection component of the due process clause of the fifth amendment. The district court applied the rational basis test and held that the statute satisfied this constitutional standard. We affirm.

The SSA determined that Yost was not eligible for Social Security benefits for surviving divorced spouses because of the operation of section 202(7) of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. § 402(7) (1976). This section provides that if “any person” is entitled to survivor’s benefits under the Railroad Retirement Act, then no survivor’s benefits shall be paid to “any person” on the basis of the earnings of an employee insured under both Acts.
provisions: Fifth Amendment — equal protection component; 42 U.S.C. § 402(7) (1976)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710 (8th Cir. 1983)
interps.summary: The court held that a parent has a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of her child. Because the government relocated and concealed the child without providing any opportunity for the parent to challenge that action, the court found a due-process issue. It further held that the domestic-relations exception did not bar federal-question jurisdiction where state remedies could not provide effective relief against federal officials.
excerpts: Parents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children. See, e.g., Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 1394, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982). We need not decide whether a parent’s visitation rights are constitutionally protected, because Donna has more than a right to visitation.

But here plaintiff got no process at all. At no time was she allowed to challenge, before some impartial authority, the government’s conclusion that it was necessary to take Mike into the WPP, and to keep him there, in order to protect Michael’s life. We can readily agree with the Marshals Service that advance notice of a person’s being taken into the program need not be given. That would destroy the whole premise of secrecy on which the Program is based. But it should have been possible to devise some kind of post-deprivation process in which Donna could be heard.

Underlying the various reasons advanced to justify the domestic-relations exception is one basic premise: There is a state forum in which the plaintiff may obtain relief. Here, the state court cannot grant effective relief to Donna Ruffalo. Michael refuses to obey the court’s custody order, and ordinary processes for discovering his whereabouts are being impeded by the action of the federal government in providing him a new identity.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bae v. Immigration & Naturalization Service, 706 F.2d 866 (8th Cir. 1983)
interps.summary: The court applied the statutory definition of “child” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), under which a child is an unmarried person under twenty-one. The definition supported the rule that marriage before entry could terminate the petitioner’s child-based immigrant status and visa eligibility.
excerpts: As explained in Corniel-Rodriguez, 22 C.F.R. § 42.122(d) is a State Department regulation that directs consular officials to warn an alien of marriageable age to whom a visa has been issued on the basis of his or her status as a child that he or she will be ineligible for admission to the United States if he or she marries prior to entering the United States. This is because § 101(b)(1) of the Immigration & Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), defines the term “child” as “an unmarried person under twenty-one years of age.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the opening language of 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), defining a child as “an unmarried person under twenty-one years of age.” That language appears verbatim and remains functionally unchanged in the current text; later amendments affected other subparagraphs only.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Samore v. Graham, 726 F.2d 1268 (8th Cir. 1984)
interps.summary: The court held that ERISA’s required anti-alienation provision does not exclude a debtor’s interest in a qualified pension plan from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2). Although ERISA anti-alienation clauses may preempt state-law garnishment remedies, they do not prevent inclusion of pension benefits in the bankruptcy estate under federal bankruptcy law.
excerpts: The change in the scope of property of the estate effectuated by the new Bankruptcy Code, the legislative history of § 541(c)(2), the exemption provisions of the Code and the preemption provision of ERI-SA all convince us that Congress did not intend “applicable nonbankruptcy law” to include ERISA. Rather, Congress only intended by § 541(c)(2) to preserve the status traditional spendthrift trusts, as recognized by state law, enjoyed under the old Bankruptcy Act.

ERISA specifically provides that its provisions were not to affect the operation of other federal statutes: “Nothing in this subchapter [including 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1)] shall be construed to modify, invalidate, impair, or supersede any law of the United States ... or any rule or regulation issued under any law.” 29 U.S.C. § 1144(d). Thus, while ERISA-required anti-alienation clauses may preempt state law and preclude the use of judgment enforcement devices provided thereunder, they do hot preclude inclusion of pension benefits in a debtor’s bankruptcy estate by operation of federal law.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), the ERISA anti-alienation requirement. That provision has not been substantively amended after the 1984 decision and remains identical in wording and function; however, the supplied excerpts do not quote its language verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: First National Bank v. United States, 727 F.2d 741 (8th Cir. 1984)
interps.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-bequest rules to determine whether the surviving spouse’s noncharitable interest was treated as passing from the decedent, even though she did not take under the will. It held that an interest obtained through an election against the will or assigned in settlement of a will contest may be treated as passing from the decedent.
excerpts: Section 2055(e)(2) applies when the non-charitable and charitable interests pass “from the decedent” and are “in the same property.” As is conceded by the government, and was found by the district court, Grace did not take her interest under the will. However, property may pass from the decedent in a variety of ways other than by will. In determining whether an interest in property has passed from a decedent, 26 U.S.C. § 2056 and the regulations thereunder relating to marital bequests are applicable.

According to the Treasury Regulations a property interest gained as a result of electing against the will and a property interest assigned or surrendered to a surviving spouse as a result of the settlement of a will contest are treated as having passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse. See First National Exchange Bank of Roanoke v. United States, 335 F.2d 91, 93 n. 7 (4th Cir.1964); Allen v. United States, 359 F.2d 151, 155 (2d Cir.) cert. denied, 385 U.S. 832, 87 S.Ct. 71, 17 L.Ed.2d 67 (1966).

norms.b_justification: The decision applied the § 2056 rule concerning when an interest is treated as having passed from the decedent to the surviving spouse, reflected in current § 2056(a). The post-decision amendments identified concern other provisions—principally § 2056(b)(7), subsection (d), and paragraph (b)(10)—and do not substantively alter that passing-from-the-decedent rule.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bruner v. Dunning, 731 F.2d 527 (8th Cir. 1984)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process principles to a state custody and parental-rights proceeding. It held that alleged ineffective assistance by appointed counsel and inadequate notice did not establish a due-process violation because Bruner failed to show material prejudice, and the state-court modification also made some claimed prejudice moot.
excerpts: Deborah J. Bruner brought an action under Section 1983 of Title 42 against the Director of the Nebraska Department of Public Welfare. She asserts that she had not been afforded due process in state court proceedings concerning her parental rights. The district court, the Honorable Warren K. Urbom presiding, held that Bruner had not been denied due process of law.

In federal court Bruner alleged that she had been denied effective assistance of counsel because her appointed counsel allegedly failed to interview and call material witnesses, discuss potential defenses with her, adequately apprise her of the consequences of missing hearings, develop a plan for Bruner’s resumption of custody of her son, or to object to evidence presented at the hearings in which custody was determined. Bruner also alleges that she was denied due process because of inadequate notice of the hearings dealing with custody of her son.

The district court also rejected Bruner’s allegations of a denial of due process because of inadequate notice of the hearings. Apparently Bruner missed four of fifteen hearings. The court found that her absences did not significantly affect the state court judge’s decision that Bruner was unable to care for her son’s needs; consequently, Bruner was not prejudiced, regardless of the adequacy of the notice.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Holley v. Heckler, 734 F.2d 401 (8th Cir. 1984)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii) to determine whether Rose Marie Holley qualified as the deceased wage earner’s child for survivor benefits. It held that substantial evidence established both Martin’s biological paternity and the required living-with-or-support relationship with Holley’s mother.
excerpts: The sole question on this appeal is whether substantial evidence supports the decision of the Secretary of Health and Human Services that Rose Marie Holley is not entitled to child survivor benefits as the child of Raymond Martin, Jr., deceased, under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii). Under that section and administrative interpretation, Holley could claim benefits as Martin’s child by presenting satisfactory evidence that he was her biological father and that he lived with or contributed to the support of her mother at the time of his death.

norms.b_justification: Holley interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii), concerning proof of parentage for child survivor benefits. The post-decision amendments listed do not substantively alter that clause; the 1984 amendment to subsection (h)(3) was technical and the 1990 and 2004 amendments addressed other provisions. Thus the interpreted language remains identical in function to the current provision.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Horton v. Marshall Public Schools, 769 F.2d 1323 (8th Cir. 1985)
interps.summary: The court held that the school district’s policy violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause by creating an irrebuttable presumption that children without a parent or legal guardian residing in the district were not domiciled there, despite reasonable alternative means of determining domicile. The court rejected the claim that the policy impermissibly burdened a nontraditional family-living arrangement because it did not require children to live with a parent or legal guardian.
excerpts: rict court’s interpretation of the term “domicile” in the school attendance context to mean “residence”, there is no authority for so limiting a child’s domicile under Arkansas case law. See Spriggs v. Altheimer, Arkansas School District No. 22, supra. Accordingly, it is not “universally true” that children who do not have a parent or legal guardian living in the Marshall school district are not domiciled in the district (i.e. residing in the district with a present intent to remain). Since, as in Vlandis, reasonable alternative means of determining the child’s domicile exist, the Marshall school district policy creates an unconstitutional irrebuttable presumption.

3. Nontraditional Family-Living Arrangement. Plaintiffs further contend that the Marshall Public School District’s policy unconstitutionally interferes with their right to adopt a nontraditional family-living arrangement. See Moore v. City of East Cleveland, 431 U.S. 494, 506, 97 S.Ct. 1932, 1939, 52 L.Ed.2d 531 (1977). Plaintiffs reading of the school district’s policy in this regard is too broad, however, in that the district has not required minor children to actually live with a parent or legal guardian. Rather, the district has only required that a parent or legal guardian live in the Marshall school district boundaries. Thus, there is no impermissible burden on plaintiffs’ right to adopt a nontraditional family-living arrangement.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community v. City of Prior Lake, 771 F.2d 1153 (8th Cir. 1985)
interps.summary: The court applied 8 U.S.C. § 1401(b) in recognizing that Congress conferred United States citizenship on Indians as a group. It relied on that citizenship in concluding that reservation residents were part of the state and local political structure for voting purposes.
excerpts: Congress conferred United States citizenship on Indians as a group with the passage of 8 U.S.C. § 1401(b) (1982). State and local citizenship are derivatives of federal citizenship.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1401(b), concerning citizenship at birth for persons born in the United States to members of specified Indigenous tribes. The identified post-decision amendments affected only subsections (g) and (h), leaving subsection (b)'s wording and function unchanged; the excerpts are paraphrased rather than verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Bohn v. County of Dakota, 772 F.2d 1433 (8th Cir. 1985)
interps.summary: The court held that the privacy and autonomy of the parent-child relationship constitute protectible liberty interests under the Due Process Clause. It therefore evaluated the procedures used to determine child abuse under the Mathews v. Eldridge framework, balancing the family interest, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the government's interests.
excerpts: The privacy and autonomy of familial relationships involved in a case like this are unarguably among the protectible interests which due process protects. We can conceive of no more important relationship, no more basic bond in American society, than the tie between parent and child.

Having identified the protectible interests at stake, we next turn to the procedural protections that are due under Minn. Stat.Ann. § 626.556. To assist the courts in evaluating the propriety of such procedures, the Supreme Court in Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 96 S.Ct. 893, 47 L.Ed.2d 18 (1976), identified three factors:
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Stokes v. Heckler, 773 F.2d 990 (8th Cir. 1985)
interps.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s widow’s-benefit provisions to determine whether Everlene qualified as a surviving divorced wife. It held that marital validity for benefit purposes is determined under state law and reversed the denial of benefits.
excerpts: The Secretary concluded that Everlene is not a surviving divorced wife of Bossie Stokes (Stokes) within the meaning of the Social Security Act’s widow’s benefits provisions, 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e), 416(d), 416(h)(1)(A); and that Everlene therefore is not entitled to receive benefits on the basis of Stokes’ earnings record. We reverse.

Under the Social Security Act, if a woman divorces a man after ten or more years of marriage and does not remarry, and if her ex-husband then dies fully insured, she may be entitled to receive widow’s benefits on her ex-husband’s earnings record upon reaching age sixty. 42 U.S.C. §§ 402(e), 416(d). The validity of the marriage for purposes of entitlement to widow’s benefits is tested by state law. 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(1)(A). Accordingly, the question Everlene presented to the Secretary and to the district court was whether she had been validly married to Stokes under the law of Arkansas.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted the eligibility of a surviving divorced wife under 42 U.S.C. § 402(e), including the cross-references to the definitions in §§ 416(d) and 416(h)(1)(A), particularly the state-law validity of the marriage. The later amendments listed for § 402(e) altered other provisions and did not change the surviving-divorced-wife definition or the state-law marriage-validity rule, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(d)'s ten-year marriage requirement for a surviving divorced wife, together with § 416(h)(1)(A)'s state-law marriage-validity rule and § 402(e)'s widow’s-benefits provision. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively alter those provisions; amendments to other subsections of § 416 are harmless, so the interpreted language remains identical in function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: In re Societe Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, 782 F.2d 120 (8th Cir. 1986)
interps.summary: The court construed the Hague Evidence Convention as providing the governing, exclusive procedures for obtaining evidence located in the territory of a foreign signatory. It emphasized that the Convention was intended to reconcile the foreign state’s judicial sovereignty with the forum litigant’s need for evidence.
excerpts: In response to this problem, the Hague Convention was designed to accommodate the civil law signatories’ concerns for judicial sovereignty with the needs of litigants to collect evidence within those countries. To effectuate this purpose, the drafters of the Hague Convention provided procedures for the taking of evidence that would be “tolerable” in the country where the discovery takes place and “utilizable” in the forum country.

Of course, the civil law signatories’ concern for judicial sovereignty would only be threatened when discovery procedures that are typically considered a judicial function are actually undertaken within the signatories’ borders by a private party.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403 (8th Cir. 1986)
interps.summary: The court recognized that parents possess a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. It held that the alleged reduction of visitation and foster-placement decisions did not establish a substantive due process violation, and that Missouri’s available post-deprivation procedures provided constitutionally adequate protection for the parents’ interests.
excerpts: This court has previously recognized that “[pjarents have a fundamental ‘liberty interest’ in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983) (citing Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982)). “That [the Fitzgeralds may have] been deprived of a constitutionally protected right, of course, does not answer the whole question of whether [they have] a claim for relief. [They] must also show that [they were] deprived of the right without due process of law.” Id.

The Fitzgeralds’ procedural due process claim is based on the defendants’ failure to provide the Fitzgeralds with a hearing prior to reducing their periodic visits with Wisa or prior to permitting Wisa to remain with her DFS-selected foster parent. We recognize the possibility that visitation and placement decisions may be subject to due process scrutiny, as such decisions may infringe upon a parent’s interest in the “care, custody, and management of their child.” Santosky v. Kramer, supra, 455 U.S. at 753, 102 S.Ct. at 1394-95.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Gorrie v. Bowen, 809 F.2d 508 (8th Cir. 1987)
interps.summary: The court held that Congress could condition federal AFDC funding on the family-unit filing regulation under its Spending Clause authority, despite the States’ traditional role in child-support matters. It further held that conflicting state child-support restrictions were preempted where they substantially interfered with the federal scheme, and that the regulation did not directly and substantially infringe protected family choices or violate due process.
excerpts: The spending clause gives Congress the “Power To lay and collect Taxes * * * to * * * provide for the * * * general Welfare of the United States.” U.S. Const, art. I, § 8, cl. 1. In the course of exercising its spending power Congress unquestionably may impose conditions on the receipt of federal funds by the states.

Our review under the supremacy clause takes on a special character because of the involvement of state family law, which will be overridden by conflicting federal law only when Congress has “ ‘positively required’ ” such a result “ ‘by direct enactment,’ ” Hisquierdo v. Hisquierdo, 439 U.S. 572, 581, 99 S.Ct. 802, 808, 59 L.Ed.2d 1 (1979) (quoting Wetmore v. Markoe, 196 U.S. 68, 77, 25 S.Ct. 172, 176, 49 L.Ed. 390 (1904)), and when the state law does “ ‘major damage’ ” to a “ ‘clear and substantial’ ” federal interest.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437 (8th Cir. 1987)
interps.summary: The court recognized that parents and children possess a constitutionally protected liberty interest in their care and companionship. It held that this interest is not absolute and that damages claims arising from the summary separation of children from parents were barred by qualified immunity where the legality of the conduct was legitimately uncertain.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has recognized a liberty interest which parents and children have in the care and companionship of each other. See, e.g., Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258 (1983) (“ * * * the Court has found that the relationship of love and duty in a recognized family unit is an interest in liberty entitled to constitutional protection.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Williams v. St. Louis County, 812 F.2d 1079 (8th Cir. 1987)
interps.summary: The court held that when an indigent plaintiff presents a non-frivolous state-law claim, denying in forma pauperis status or comparable fee relief without apparent justification makes an otherwise adequate state postdeprivation remedy inadequate. The court relied on this access-to-courts principle to vacate dismissal of the plaintiff’s § 1983 action.
excerpts: To refuse to waive filing fees and grant in forma pauperis status in these circumstances raises concerns of a constitutional magnitude even outside the context of an assessment of the adequacy of state remedies under Parratt. See Boddie v. Connecticut, 401 U.S. 371, 91 S.Ct. 780, 28 L.Ed.2d 113 (1971); United States v. Kras, 409 U.S. 434, 93 S.Ct. 631, 34 L.Ed.2d 626 (1973). We need not address those concerns here, however; instead, we hold only that where an indigent plaintiff presents a non-frivolous state-law claim, the denial of in forma pauperis status or similar relief for no apparent reason renders an otherwise-adequate postdeprivation remedy inadequate under Parratt.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Harpole v. Arkansas Department of Human Services, 820 F.2d 923 (8th Cir. 1987)
interps.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment due-process principles concerning familial association and recognized that parents and children may possess a liberty interest in each other’s companionship. It held, however, that Harpole did not establish a constitutionally protected loss arising from the death of her adult son, particularly where the alleged governmental interference was indirect.
excerpts: Both the Supreme Court and this court have recognized a liberty interest which parents and children have in each other’s companionship. See, e.g., Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983); Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462-63 (8th Cir.1987). Familial relationships have been protected from many forms of governmental intrusion.

The First Circuit, in Ortiz v. Burgos, 807 F.2d 6 (1st Cir.1986), divided constitutionally protected interests in familial relationships into two categories. In the first category are cases protecting the right to make private decisions affecting the family, such as whether to bear children. “The emphasis in these cases on choice suggests that the right is one of preemption; rather than an absolute right to a certain family relationship, family members have the right, when confronted with the state’s attempt to make choices for them, to choose for themselves.” Id. at 8. The second category contains cases dealing with governmental attempts to directly affect the parent-child relationship by means such as determining paternity or terminating parental rights.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Estate of Brandon v. Commissioner, 828 F.2d 493 (8th Cir. 1987)
interps.summary: The court held that a settlement qualifies for the estate-tax marital deduction only to the extent it reflects an enforceable surviving-spouse claim under properly interpreted state law. It remanded for an independent determination whether Arkansas’s gender-based dower-election statute was constitutional under the Equal Protection Clause at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr.
excerpts: Specifically, we agree that “under even the most narrow reading of Bosch, either a good faith settlement or a judgment of a lower state court must be based on an enforceable right, under state law properly interpreted, in order to qualify as ‘passing’ pursuant to the estate tax marital deduction.” Ahmanson, supra, 674 F.2d at 775.

Bosch and Ahmanson support the conclusion that the Tax Court was required, in this instance, to make an independent determination as to the enforceability of Chanoy Brandon’s dower claims against the estate under state law at the time the settlement was reached. Specifically, the Tax Court was required to consider the constitutionality of the Arkansas dower statute at the time of settlement, in light of Orr v. Orr. Having carefully reviewed the Tax Court’s opinion, we find that the Tax Court failed to do so.

The Tax Court’s reliance upon Estate of Barrett v. Commissioner, supra, holding that the test for determining the enforceability of the surviving spouse’s claims against the estate is whether or not the settlement agreement was made as the result of good faith, arm’s-length negotiations, was improper, because that case appears to have been overruled sub silentio by Bosch. We therefore remand for a determination of the constitutionality of ARK.STAT.ANN. § 60-501 at the time the settlement was reached.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a), particularly whether an enforceable state-law interest “passes” to the surviving spouse for purposes of the marital deduction. The later amendments listed affect other subsections and do not alter § 2056(a) or its relevant function; the Equal Protection issue likewise does not change that statutory language.

provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Equal Protection Clause

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Sherrill ex rel. Sherrill v. Bowen, 835 F.2d 166 (8th Cir. 1987)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h) to determine whether the applicant qualified as the deceased insured wage-earner’s “child” for Social Security surviving-child benefits. It affirmed the denial because the evidence did not establish paternity under Missouri intestacy law or satisfy the statutory routes for establishing child status.
excerpts: The Social Security Act (Act), 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(1), establishes the criteria for entitlement to child’s insurance benefits. It provides that every “child” of an individual who dies insured under the Act is entitled to benefits if the child has applied for them, is unmarried, under 18, and was dependent on the deceased insured at the time of the latter’s death. Id. Title 42 U.S.C. § 416(h) sets forth the requirements for determining whether an applicant is the child of an insured. On appeal Sherill argues that Lamarko is entitled to benefits under § 416(h)(2)(A) or § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii).

Under § 416(h)(2)(A), benefits are available to those children who would inherit from the deceased wage-earner under the intestate laws of the state in which the wage-earner was domiciled at his death. Roosevelt Robinson was domiciled in the state of Missouri at the time of his death. Thus, the relevant statute is Mo.Rev.Stat. § 474.060(2) (1986), which provides in relevant part: 2. [A] person born out of wedlock is a child of the mother. That person is also a child of the father, if ... (2) the paternity is established by an adjudication before the death of the father, or is established thereafter by clear and convincing proof

norms.b_justification: Sherrill interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and § 416(h)(3)(C). The listed post-decision amendments to subsection (h) altered only paragraph (1) and did not amend either provision at issue, so their wording and function remain unchanged in the current version.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Murphy v. Arkansas, 852 F.2d 1039 (8th Cir. 1988)
interps.summary: The court rejected the parents’ claim that the Fourteenth Amendment gives them a fundamental right to supervise their children’s education free from state testing requirements. It also applied rational-basis review to Arkansas’s differing regulation of home schools and private schools, upholding the classification.
excerpts: Second, we find no persuasive arguments advanced that there is a fundamental right of parents to supervise their children’s education to the extent that the Murphys contend. The recognition of such a right would fly directly in the face of those cases in which the Supreme Court has recognized the broad power of the state to compel school attendance and regulate curriculum and teacher certification. See Board of Education v. Allen, 392 U.S. at 245-46, 88 S.Ct. at 1927-28; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 534, 45 S.Ct. 571, 573, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925). Thus, again, strict scrutiny cannot be invoked in this case.

Given that strict scrutiny analysis does not apply, we move to the question of whether Arkansas has a rational reason to subject home schooling to regulatory requirements, while at the same time freeing private schools from virtually any regulation. This step by the legislature in Arkansas may at first glance offend common sense, and, sitting as a legislature, we might not have made this same decision. However, our job is not to sit as a legislature and the constitutional standard of rationality under the equal protection clause is a relaxed one.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Director, Office of Workers' Compensation Programs v. Logan, 868 F.2d 285 (8th Cir. 1989)
interps.summary: The court applied the definition of “surviving divorced wife” in 42 U.S.C. § 416(d)(2), as incorporated into the Black Lung Benefits Act’s eligibility provision. The dispute was ultimately resolved on the separate dependency requirement: Social Security benefits were not contributions made from the miner’s property.
excerpts: To be eligible for black lung benefits, a surviving divorced spouse of a coal miner must establish that she was dependent on the miner the month before the miner died. Section 402(e) of the Act, 30 U.S.C. § 902(e), provides in pertinent part:

e) The term “widow” includes * * * a “surviving divorced wife” as defined in section 416(d)(2) of Title 42 who for the month preceding the month in which the miner died, was receiving at least one-half of her support * * * or was receiving substantial contributions from the miner (pursuant to a written agreement) or there was in effect a court order for substantial contributions to her support from the miner at the time of his death.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(d)(2), defining a “surviving divorced wife” by requiring a woman to have been married to the deceased individual for at least 10 years before the divorce became effective. That provision appears substantively unchanged in the current text, and the listed post-decision amendments do not amend subsection (d); the method is functional-review because the excerpt does not quote the provision verbatim.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Luke ex rel. Luke v. Bowen, 868 F.2d 974 (8th Cir. 1989)
interps.summary: The court affirmed denial of surviving child’s insurance benefits, holding that an illegitimate child must establish a biological relationship to the deceased wage earner to qualify under either § 416(h)(2)(A) or § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I). The deceased wage earner’s written acknowledgment was insufficient where substantial evidence showed he could not have been the child’s biological father.
excerpts: Specifically, the district court found that the AU correctly determined that in order for an illegitimate child to be eligible for benefits under either 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) or § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I) he must first establish a biological relationship to the wage earner.

4.Scott Luke was not entitled to benefits under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I), because Groth’s written acknowledgment that Scott was his son was insufficient in light of evidence that Scott had no biological relationship to Groth.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and § 416(h)(3)(C)(i)(I), concerning the need to establish a biological relationship for an illegitimate child’s benefits eligibility. The listed amendments after 1989 do not alter either provision; the 2004 changes concern other subsections, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: DeMent ex rel. DeMent v. Oglala Sioux Tribal Court, 874 F.2d 510 (8th Cir. 1989)
interps.summary: The court applied the PKPA and held, following Thompson v. Thompson, that 28 U.S.C. § 1738A does not create an implied federal cause of action to resolve conflicting custody decisions; the claim should be raised in the subsequent custody proceeding. The court also held that exercising personal jurisdiction over a nonmember, nonresident parent in a tribal custody proceeding may violate due process under the Indian Civil Rights Act, analogizing to Kulko.
excerpts: The Supreme Court has held that, in an action for child support, exercising in personam jurisdiction over a nonresident nondomiciliary parent of a minor child domiciled within a state may violate the due process under the federal Constitution. Kulko v. California Superior Court, 436 U.S. 84, 101, 98 S.Ct. 1690, 1701, 56 L.Ed.2d 132 (1978) (the Supreme Court refused to enforce a California child support decree because the father’s contacts with the state were too attenuated to satisfy traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice).

Similarly, we believe that a tribal court exercising in personam jurisdiction over a nonmember nonresident parent of a minor child domiciled within the Indian reservation may violate due process under section 1302(8) of the ICRA. We believe that DeMent may have a valid due process claim under the ICRA.

norms.b_justification: The decision construed 28 U.S.C. § 1738A, including subsection (f), concerning a State court’s authority to modify a custody determination made by a court of another State. Subsection (f) was not amended after the 1989 decision, and the later amendments affected other provisions without changing the interpreted language or its function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Lux ex rel. Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064 (8th Cir. 1989)
interps.summary: The court applied the substantive due process principle that parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. It considered that asserted right in reviewing the qualified-immunity defense to the § 1983 claim arising from the child’s separation from her father.
excerpts: Carrie alleges that her due process and liberty rights were violated when she was separated from her father as a result of DSS’s investigation and the subsequent dependency and neglect proceedings. She cites Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403 (8th Cir.1986), in which we recognized that “ ‘[pjarents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children.’ ” Id. at 407 (quoting Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983)).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Henne ex rel. Henne v. Wright, 904 F.2d 1208 (8th Cir. 1990)
interps.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment substantive-due-process principles to determine whether parents have a fundamental right to give a child at birth a surname lacking a legally established parental connection. It recognized constitutionally protected parental child-rearing interests but held that those interests are not absolute and do not establish the asserted naming right.
excerpts: Whether there is a fundamental right to give a child a surname at birth with which the child has no legally established parental connection will dictate the appropriate level of constitutional scrutiny for evaluating Neb.Rev.Stat. § 71-640.01. Specifically, if the statute significantly infringes a right deemed fundamental under the fourteenth amendment right of privacy then we must rigorously scrutinize the asserted justifications for the statute.

While Meyer and Pierce extended constitutional protection to parental decisions relating to child rearing, the parental rights recognized in those cases centered primarily around the training and education of children. For example, the law at issue in Meyer prevented parents from having their children taught in a foreign language, 262 U.S. at 396-403, 43 S.Ct. at 626-28, and the law at issue in Pierce prevented parents from sending their children to non-public schools, 268 U.S. at 529-36, 45 S.Ct. at 571-74.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Walker v. Sullivan, 905 F.2d 1186 (8th Cir. 1990)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii) in determining whether the claimant qualified as the deceased wage earner’s child for surviving-child Social Security benefits. It affirmed the denial because the evidence did not establish that the wage earner was living with or contributing to the child’s support when he died.
excerpts: Betty Walker (Walker), for her minor daughter April Denise Walker (April), appeals from the district court’s order affirming the decision of the Secretary of Health and Human Services (Secretary) denying April’s application for surviving child’s benefits under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii) of the Social Security Act. For the reasons discussed below, we affirm.

In deciding that the conditions for entitlement to child’s benefits had not been met, the AU stated with regard to 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii): While the evidence includes statements by the claimant’s mother and from several of the wage earner’s friends and relatives indicating that the wage earner admitted orally he was the father of the child and gave money to the child, the evidence does not show that the wage earner was living with or contributing to the support of the child at the time the wage earner died.

norms.b_justification: Walker interpreted the support/cohabitation requirement in 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(3)(C)(ii)—that the wage earner was living with or contributing to the child’s support at death. The post-decision amendments identified do not substantively alter that provision; the later subsection (h) change merely replaces “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security,” which does not affect the interpreted requirement.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Schweiss v. Chrysler Motors Corp., 922 F.2d 473 (8th Cir. 1990)
interps.summary: The court rejected Chrysler’s argument that 42 U.S.C. § 660(c) preempted state-law claims providing the asserted relief. It found no such preemptive intent in the statutory text or legislative history.
excerpts: Nothing in the text of the statute shows such an intent. Further, Chrysler does not point us to any suggestion in the legislative history of 42 U.S.C. § 660(c) that Congress intended to preempt state law actions that allow such relief.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Steen v. Commissioner, 923 F.2d 603 (8th Cir. 1991)
interps.summary: The court applied §§ 71 and 215 to determine whether payments made to the taxpayer’s former wife were deductible alimony or nondeductible child-support or property-settlement payments. It held that the payments were in the nature of a property settlement and therefore were not includible under § 71 or deductible under § 215.
excerpts: 26 U.S.C. § 215(a) (1982) (amended 1984) stated: In the case of a husband described in section 71, there shall be allowed as a deduction amounts includible under section 71 in the gross income of his wife, payment of which is made within the husband’s taxable year. 26 U.S.C. § 71(a) (1982) required a divorced or separated wife to include in gross income all payments received from her husband in discharge of an obligation imposed on the husband under the divorce decree or a written instrument incident to such divorce or separation.
