Where, however, payments discharged an obligation to support minor children, section 71(b), or represented installment payments discharging a property settlement, section 71(c)(1), such payments were not considered income to the wife under section 71 or deductible by the husband under section 215.

We have carefully considered the argument of the Steens, and conclude that the tax court did not err in holding that the payments to Janet were in the nature of a property settlement rather than support, and accordingly not deductible by the Steens.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Jackson v. Rapps, 947 F.2d 332 (8th Cir. 1991)
interps.summary: The court held that Missouri’s policy of setting an AFDC reimbursement debt equal to all public assistance paid violated Title IV-D requirements. Under 42 U.S.C. §§ 654(13) and 656(a)(2), when no court order establishes support, the state must determine the obligation using a federally approved formula and the criteria required by federal regulations.
excerpts: The amount of the obligation is set by a court order for support, unless there is no court order covering support rights. 42 U.S.C. § 656(a)(2). In that instance, the obligation shall be “determined by the State in accordance with a formula approved by the Secretary.” 42 U.S.C. § 656(a)(2)(B).

We are convinced that the Director’s policy in setting the amount of state debt as the total amount of public assistance paid out violates federal regulations governing the AFDC program. Here, statutes and regulations covering the AFDC program require that the states follow criteria set forth in 45 C.F.R. § 302.53(a). 42 U.S.C. § 654(13) (1988) provides: “... the State will comply with such other requirements and standards as the Secretary [of Health and Human Services] determines to be necessary to the establishment of an effective program for ... obtaining support orders, and collecting support payments.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 656(a)(2) and § 656(a)(2)(B), requiring the obligation to be set by a support order or, absent one, by a State formula approved by the Secretary; that operative language appears verbatim in the current text. Although § 656(a)(2)(B) was later amended to change “Secretary, and” to “Secretary.”, the change was technical and did not alter the provision’s wording or function as applied in Jackson v. Rapps.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Arkansas Blue Cross & Blue Shield v. St. Mary's Hospital, Inc., 947 F.2d 1341 (8th Cir. 1991)
interps.summary: The court considered ERISA’s anti-assignment provision for pension benefits in analyzing preemption. It held that the provision’s express prohibition on pension-benefit assignments did not imply that states could regulate assignments of ERISA welfare benefits, and that the provision did not control the assignment-statute issue.
excerpts: Arguably, one such provision is 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), which provides that “each pension plan shall provide that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated.” Although the Supreme Court found this provision relevant in addressing ERISA preemption of state garnishment laws, Mackey, 486 U.S. at 837, 108 S.Ct. at 2189, the Court’s analysis does not apply to assignment statutes.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), including the requirement that each pension plan provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. This language appears verbatim in the current text, and the listed later amendments concern other provisions of subsection (d), not § 1056(d)(1).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Zeien v. Palmer, 955 F.2d 506 (8th Cir. 1992)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 654(5), as implemented by HHS regulations, to uphold the treatment of a child-support payment as reimbursement for AFDC benefits already paid when that payment rendered the family ineligible. The court also recognized the resulting hardship and required corrective AFDC payments and automatic reinstatement when continuing support payments did not materialize.
excerpts: In 1982, Congress amended the Social Security Act to require the state child support collection agency to use the payment that rendered the family ineligible to reimburse the state for AFDC paid in the month for which the support payment was collected. Tax Equity & Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982, Pub.L. No. 97-248, § 173(a), 96 Stat. 403 (1982) (codified at 42 U.S.C. § 654(5) (1988)) [hereinafter TEFRA]. Congress intended to eliminate double payment to an AFDC family for any single month, and to ensure reimbursement to the state and federal government for AFDC already paid in the month before the support was collected and known to make the family ineligible.

The lack of income in June 1988 that prompted Zeien to commence this action thus was the product of the TEFRA amendment prohibiting direct payment to the family of a child support collection sufficient to render the family ineligible for AFDC. See supra note 2 (describing distribution of Zeien’s April 1988 child support payment pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 654(5) and 45 C.F.R. § 302.51). Even if HHS regulations permitted IDHS to make a best estimate of the likelihood of continued child support before terminating AFDC benefits, distribution of child support collections as required under TEFRA would produce a similar lack of income whenever the agency wrongly predicted that child support would continue.

norms.b_justification: Zeien interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 654(5)’s requirement that support payments subject to an effective assignment be paid to the State for statutory distribution rather than directly to the AFDC family. Current § 654(5)(A) retains that same operative requirement; the changed cross-reference and added notice language do not alter the interpreted rule’s function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Zahradnik v. Sullivan, 966 F.2d 355 (8th Cir. 1992)
interps.summary: The court held that, under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), the Social Security Secretary must apply the law of the insured wage earner’s domicile governing intestate succession. Applying Oregon law, the court concluded that paternity could be established in the Social Security benefits proceeding without a prior independent state paternity action, and that the claimant had established paternity for inheritance purposes.
excerpts: A request for benefits is to be evaluated under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) (1988), which holds that when considering whether or not a child is to receive insurance benefits, “the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which the insured individual ... was domiciled at the time of his death.

We find that the AU misconstrued Oregon law and hold that under Oregon law petitioner may establish his right to inherit in a proceeding for social security benefits without having first had paternity established in an independent state paternity suit. We further find that Zahradnik has established that Hansen was his father for purposes of inheriting under Oregon law and that substantial evidence does not exist on the record as a whole to substantiate the Secretary’s denial of benefits.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), requiring application of the law governing intestate succession in the insured individual's domicile state to determine a child's entitlement. The later amendment only replaced “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security” in subsection (h), a technical agency-title change that did not alter the provision’s wording in substance or its function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Wear v. Green, 967 F.2d 1216 (8th Cir. 1992)
interps.summary: The court applied ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement in determining whether the employee’s vested interest in the retirement plan could be included in the bankruptcy estate. It reversed the lower courts’ conclusion that the ERISA-covered plan interest was estate property.
excerpts: Wal-Mart maintains a profit-sharing plan for its employees. The plan is funded solely from contributions from Wal-Mart, and annual contributions are made at the sole discretion of Wal-Mart’s board of directors. The plan does not accept employee contributions, though under limited circumstances employees can rollover funds from other retirement plans into the Wal-Mart plan.

As required by ERISA, see 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d) (1988), the plan contains restrictions on alienation and assignment of plan benefits. Employees can receive distributions only upon the employee’s death, disability, retirement, or termination.

both appeal the district court’s affirmance of the bankruptcy court’s decision that an individual’s interest in a retirement plan covered by ERISA is part of that individual’s bankruptcy estate. We reverse and remand.

norms.b_justification: Wear v. Green interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), requiring pension plans to provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. That language and function remain unchanged in the current text; the later amendments identified affect other provisions of subsection (d) and do not alter § 1056(d)(1).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Iannacone v. Northern States Power Co., 974 F.2d 88 (8th Cir. 1992)
interps.summary: The court applied ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement to pension plans whose provisions restricted the alienation and assignment of plan benefits. It held that the debtor’s interests in those ERISA-qualified plans could be excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).
excerpts: Each pension plan contains an anti-alienation provision restricting alienation and assignment of plan benefits. See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1). In October 1989 the debtor filed a Chapter 7 petition for bankruptcy. He claimed his interests in the pension plans were exempt and estimated their value at about $28,000.00.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), requiring pension plans to provide that benefits may not be assigned or alienated. That language appears verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments cited affected other provisions of subsection (d), not paragraph (1).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Lannan v. Maul, 979 F.2d 627 (8th Cir. 1992)
interps.summary: The court applied the narrow domestic-relations exception, holding that it does not bar federal jurisdiction over a collateral third-party beneficiary contract claim merely because the contract arose from a divorce-related property settlement. The court also considered whether Younger abstention was warranted because related family-law proceedings were pending in state court.
excerpts: The domestic relations exception, upon which the district court relied to decline jurisdiction, was recently addressed by the United States Supreme Court in the case of Ankenbrandt v. Richards, - U.S. -, 112 S.Ct. 2206, 119 L.Ed.2d 468 (1992) (Ankenbrandt). We held this appeal in abeyance pending the Supreme Court’s decision in Ankenbrandt. In Ankenbrandt, the Supreme Court determined that it was “unwilling to cast aside an understood rule that has been recognized for nearly a century and a half” and held that it would continue to recognize the domestic relations exception to federal jurisdiction. Id. 112 S.Ct. at 2210. However, the Court concluded that a tort action arising out of the domestic relations of the parties did not fall within the domestic relations exception.

Thus, we conclude that the domestic relations exception, as articulated by the Supreme Court in Ankenbrandt, is a narrow one. Id. at 2215 n. 6 (Noting that better reasoned views among Courts of Appeals have similarly limited the domestic relations exception). The case at bar is similar to Ankenbrandt. The issues presented here do not involve a domestic relations dispute between a feuding couple concerning a divorce, alimony, or child custody decree. Rather, it concerns a third-party beneficiary claim based on contract law. We hold, therefore, that the district court erred in holding that it lacked jurisdiction because the domestic relations exception does not encompass collateral issues, such as the alleged breach of contract presented here.

Although the federal district court did not specifically invoke the abstention doctrine announced in Younger v. Harris, as an alternative ground for its holding, the district court concluded that the issues raised were substantially related to and intertwined with issues pending before state courts. See page 630. Lannan argues, however, that the district court erred in declining jurisdiction because neither he, as conservator, nor Ashley Brewer, is a party to any other state court litigation or was a party to the divorce litigation between her parents. Moreover, Lannan argues this is a breach of contract claim which has no significant relationship to any action pending in state court.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Eldridge v. Sullivan, 980 F.2d 499 (8th Cir. 1992)
interps.summary: The court applied the Social Security Act’s statutory rules for determining whether a nonmarital child qualifies as the deceased wage earner’s child for child’s insurance benefits. It held that the evidence was insufficient to establish entitlement under the applicable § 416(h) provisions and reversed the award of benefits.
excerpts: Appellant Kay Eldridge appeals from a final order entered in the District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas affirming the decision of the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services to grant claims by Kathryn Reid Leach for child’s insurance benefits under § 216(h) of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. § 416(h). Eldridge v. Sullivan, No. PB-C-90-466, slip op. at 3, 1991 WL 325536 (E.D.Ark. Oct. 31, 1991) (Memorandum and Order). For the reasons discussed below, we reverse.

The SSA denied Leach’s application initially and on reconsideration because there was no showing that Leach’s children had received support from B.P. Eldridge. On December 4, 1987, Leach filed another application, attaching statements from her family and friends attesting that B.P. Eldridge was Matthew’s

Nor can the hearsay evidence offered in the present case even be considered substantial enough to clearly convince a factfinder that the evidence is true and admits of no reasonable doubt. Accordingly, the judgment of the district court is reversed and the case is remanded for judgment to be entered in accordance with this opinion.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) and § 416(h)(3), concerning establishment of parent-child relationship and support for child’s insurance benefits. The post-decision amendments identified do not substantively alter those provisions; the 1994 changes to subsection (h) merely replace references to the Secretary with the Commissioner, while the 2004 amendments concern subsections (c), (g), and (k).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Cooper ex rel. Cooper v. Sullivan, 985 F.2d 390 (8th Cir. 1993)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) to determine whether the claimant qualified as the deceased wage earner’s natural child for surviving child’s insurance benefits. Eligibility depended on whether the claimant could inherit the decedent’s personal property under Illinois law, including Illinois’s clear-and-convincing-evidence requirement for paternity.
excerpts: Under 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) (1988), Marvel Cooper is eligible for benefits as Marvin Thomas’s natural child if he could inherit Thomas’s personal property under the law of Illinois, the state in which Thomas was domiciled at the time of his death. Illinois law provides in relevant part: If a decedent has acknowledged paternity of an illegitimate person or if during his lifetime or after his death a decedent has been adjudged to be the father of an illegitimate person, that person is heir of his father.... If during his lifetime the decedent was adjudged to be the father of an illegitimate person by a court of competent jurisdiction, an authenticated copy of the judgment is sufficient proof of the paternity; but in all other cases 'paternity must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.

norms.b_justification: The decision construed 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), applying the state-law intestate-inheritance test to determine whether the claimant qualified as the insured’s natural child. The later 1994 amendment replacing “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security” was technical and did not alter that test’s wording or function; the 2004 amendments affected other provisions.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Coleman v. Espy, 986 F.2d 1184 (8th Cir. 1993)
interps.summary: The court distinguished civil contempt from criminal contempt by examining the substance of the proceeding and the character of the relief. Civil contempt is remedial and benefits the complainant, while criminal contempt is punitive and vindicates the court’s authority.
excerpts: Civil contempt is distinct from criminal contempt. To determine whether a contempt proceeding is civil or criminal, we must look at the substance of the proceeding and the character of the relief the proceeding will afford. Hicks v. Feiock, 485 U.S. 624, 631, 108 S.Ct. 1423, 1429, 99 L.Ed.2d 721 (1988). "If it is for civil contempt the punishment is remedial, and for the benefit of the complainant. But if it is for criminal contempt the sentence is punitive, to vindicate the authority of the court.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Buder v. United States, 7 F.3d 1382 (8th Cir. 1993)
interps.summary: The court applied the QTIP statutory requirement that the surviving spouse be entitled to all trust income, payable annually or more frequently. It did not decide whether the trust satisfied that requirement because the Government waived its challenge by failing to raise it during the audit or plead it timely.
excerpts: Assets do not qualify as QTIP unless “the surviving spouse is entitled to all the income from the property, payable annually or at more frequent intervals.” 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I) (1988). Article VI(e) of Buder’s will states only that, during the life of his widow, the “trustees shall pay over and deliver to her monthly any portion or all of the net income of the trust estate as they may in their discretion deem advisable.” The Government argues that the trustees are allowed to accumulate the trust income and, hence, the estate’s QTIP deduction was improper. We need not reach the merits of this argument, however, as we conclude that the Government waived this defense.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I), requiring that the surviving spouse be entitled to all income from the property, payable annually or more frequently. The listed post-decision amendments concern § 2056(b)(7)(C) and § 2056(b)(8), not the construed QTIP-income requirement, which remains identical in wording and function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Voss v. Shalala, 32 F.3d 1269 (8th Cir. 1994)
interps.summary: The court applied 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A) to determine whether the claimants qualified as the deceased wage earner’s children for Social Security survivor benefits. It held that Nebraska intestacy law governed their status and affirmed the finding that they were not eligible to inherit as Clarence Voss’s children.
excerpts: An applicant is entitled to surviving children’s benefits if he or she was the “natural child, legally adopted child, stepchild, ... or equitably adopted child” of a deceased wage earner. 20 C.F.R. § 404.354(a). “In determining whether an applicant is the child ... of a[n] ... insured individual ..., the Secretary shall apply such law as would be applied in determining the devolution of intestate personal property by the courts of the State in which such insured individual ... was domiciled at the time of his death.” 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 416(h)(2)(A), concerning application of the law governing intestate succession in the insured individual's State of domicile. The later amendment to subsection (h) merely replaced “Secretary” with “Commissioner of Social Security,” a technical institutional change that did not alter the provision’s wording in any substantive respect or its legal function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Whetzal v. Alderson, 32 F.3d 1302 (8th Cir. 1994)
interps.summary: The court relied on the ERISA anti-alienation requirement, as construed in Patterson v. Shumate, to explain that an ERISA-qualified plan interest may be excluded from a bankruptcy estate. The opinion contrasted that restriction with the statutory treatment of civil-service retirement benefits.
excerpts: Excluded from the bankruptcy estate is property subject to restrictions on transfer by “applicable nonbankruptcy law.” 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2). By way of illustration, in Patterson v. Shumate, — U.S.-,-, 112 S.Ct. 2242, 2248, 119 L.Ed.2d 519 (1992), the Supreme Court held that a debtor’s interest in an ERISA-qualified plan may be excluded from his estate under the Bankruptcy Code.

The Court relied on ERISA’s requirement that approved plans include a provision “ ‘that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated.’ ” Id. at-, 119 S.Ct. at 2247 (quoting 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1)).

norms.b_justification: Whetzal v. Alderson interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), including the requirement that plan benefits “may not be assigned or alienated.” That language remains verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments cited affected subsection (d)(3), not paragraph (d)(1).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Salas-Velazquez v. Immigration & Naturalization Service, 34 F.3d 705 (8th Cir. 1994)
interps.summary: The court applied § 204(c) to determine whether the petitioner’s prior marriage barred approval of his immigrant petition and adjustment of status. The court addressed whether a marriage entered into to obtain immigration benefits constituted a marriage entered into for the purpose of evading the immigration laws.
excerpts: The Board concluded that petitioner cannot meet this standard, because Section 204(c) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c), provides that no petition for immigrant status may be approved if ... the alien has previously been accorded, or has sought to be accorded, an immediate relative or preference status as a spouse of a citizen of the United States ... by reason of a marriage determined by the Attorney General to have been entered into for the purpose of evading the immigration laws.

There is no question that petitioner entered into his first marriage for the purpose of obtaining immigration benefits. He concedes as much. This is not the same thing, he argues, as evasion of the immigration laws. It is merely avoidance. We can understand that a person could contract a marriage with the knowledge that immigration benefits would result and for the purpose of obtaining such benefits, at least partly, without the transaction’s being considered an e

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c), which bars approval of a petition based on a marriage determined to have been entered into to evade the immigration laws. The supplied current-text excerpt does not include subsection (c), so the language is not verbatim available for comparison; however, the amendment history identifies no later amendment to subsection (c), and the 1994 amendment affected subsection (a)(1) only.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Rydder v. Rydder, 49 F.3d 369 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court held that an ICARA return proceeding determines only whether the child was wrongfully removed or retained under Hague Convention article 3, rather than adjudicating the underlying custody merits. It further held that respondents may invoke the Convention’s affirmative defenses under articles 12, 13, and 20, but those exceptions must be construed narrowly.
excerpts: Article 19 of the Convention and ICARA, 42 U.S.C. § 11601(b)(4), do not allow a court applying the Convention to adjudicate the merits of any underlying custody claims. Rather, in an action for the return of a child to the habitual residence, a petitioner must prove only that the child was removed or retained “wrongfully,” as that term is defined in Article 3 of the Hague Convention. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).

A respondent who opposes the return of a child may advance any of the affirmative defenses to return listed in Articles 12,13, or 20 of the Hague Convention. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2). We believe, however, that a court applying the Hague Convention should construe these exceptions narrowly. See Friedrich v. Friedrich, 983 F.2d at 1403.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Northrup King Co. v. Compania Productora Semillas Algodoneras Selectas, S.A., 51 F.3d 1383 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court applied Article 3 of the Hague Service Convention to the transmittal of the request for service abroad, including forwarding the request and accompanying judicial documents to the Spanish Ministry of Justice for service in Spain.
excerpts: On the day of filing, Northrup King’s attorneys and a deputy clerk of district court signed a document entitled “Request for Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents.” Pursuant to Article 3 of the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters, February 10, 1969, 70 UST 361 (“Hague Convention”), Northrup King forwarded the document to the Spanish Ministry of Justice, with two copies of the summons and complaint, a Spanish language translation of the complaint and a “Summary” of the documents to be served.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Nunez-Escudero v. Tice-Menley, 58 F.3d 374 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court applied ICARA’s burden-allocation provisions, requiring the petitioner to prove by a preponderance that the child was removed from his habitual residence and the respondent to establish the Article 13(b) exception by clear and convincing evidence. It held that the district court erred by refusing to determine habitual residence before denying return based on grave risk.
excerpts: Under the Convention, as implemented by the Act, Nunez-Escudero must initially prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Tice-Menley removed their son from his “habitual residence.” 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1). If Nunez-Escudero meets this burden, Tice-Menley must show by clear and convincing evidence the applicability of one of the exceptions set forth in Articles 13b or 20 of the Convention. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2).

The district court did not decide whether Tice-Menley removed the baby from his habitual residence. Instead, it refused to order the baby’s return because Tice-Menley established one of the Article 13b exceptions. Specifically, the court determined that there was a grave risk that the return of the child would expose him to physical and psychological harm and place him in an intolerable situation. See Art. 13b, Convention; 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(2)(A).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Amerson ex rel. M.H. v. Iowa, 59 F.3d 92 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court held that the mother’s habeas petition primarily asserted her own parental right to custody, rather than the child’s liberty interests. Because a parental-rights claim cannot establish federal habeas jurisdiction under these circumstances, the district court properly dismissed the petition.
excerpts: Particularly when a habeas petition is brought by a parent seeking the release of a child from state custody, the action may really involve an assertion of the parent’s rights, not the liberty interests of the child. See Lehman, 458 U.S. at 511, 102 S.Ct. at 3237 (“Ms. Lehman simply seeks to relitigate, through federal habeas, not any liberty interest of her sons, but the interest in her own parental rights.
Thus, we conclude Amerson’s action is merely an assertion of her right to custody of M.H., which cannot form the basis for habeas jurisdiction. See Lehman, 458 U.S. at 515-16,102 S.Ct. at 3239-40.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Manzano v. South Dakota Department of Social Services, 60 F.3d 505 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court recognized that parents have a Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children and in familial integrity. It held that the interest is not absolute and is limited by the compelling governmental interest in protecting minor children, particularly during child-abuse investigations.
excerpts: Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.) (Myers) (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983)), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828, 108 S.Ct. 97, 98 L.Ed.2d 58 (1987); see Lux by Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064, 1066-67 (8th Cir.1989) (Lux); Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1983). However, we have at the same time indicated that this right is not absolute.

As we stated in Myers, “the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” 810 F.2d at 1462. Moreover, as the First Circuit has correctly noted, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations.” Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1, 8 (1st Cir.1993) (Watterson).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, Due Process Clause

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Equitable Life Assurance Society v. Crysler, 66 F.3d 944 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision applies to pension plans, not employee welfare benefit plans such as the life-insurance plan at issue. Therefore, the former wife’s claim under the divorce decree was not barred merely because the decree was not a qualified domestic relations order, and the case was remanded for application of applicable state insurance and family-law principles.
excerpts: 1. ERISA’s anti-alienation provision does not bar Phyllis’s claim. We deal here with an “employee welfare benefit plan,” not an “employee pension benefit plan.” 29 U.S.C. §§ 1002(1), (2)(A). In many respects, Congress elected to regulate welfare benefit plans less rigorously.

Because the anti-alienation provision does not apply to welfare plan benefits, Phyllis’s divorce decree need not be a QDRO to avoid that provision. Carland v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., 935 F.2d 1114 (10th Cir.), cert. denied, 502 U.S. 1020, 112 S.Ct. 670, 116 L.Ed.2d 761 (1991), on which the district court relied, is not to the contrary.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and the QDRO exception in § 1056(d)(3)(A), concluding that the anti-alienation rule applies to pension plans, not welfare benefit plans, and therefore does not bar the claim. Those provisions remain substantively unchanged; the later amendments affected § 1056(d)(3)(B) and other provisions, not the language or function construed here.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Shangreau v. Babbitt, 68 F.3d 208 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court applied intermediate scrutiny to WELSA’s different treatment of nonmarital children seeking to inherit by representation through their fathers. It held that the paternal inheritance limitation was substantially related to the federal interest in accurately and efficiently resolving heirship claims, because of the distinctive problems of proving paternity.
excerpts: As in Lalli v. Lalli, the peculiar problems of proof of paternity as opposed to maternity justify the different treatment of paternal inheritance by illegitimate children under WELSA. Refusing to expand heirship status to include illegitimate children claiming by right of representation through their fathers is substantially related to the federal government’s important interest in accurately and efficiently settling the claims involving the White Earth Reservation allotments.
provisions: Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause (equal-protection component)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Ebmeier v. Stump, 70 F.3d 1012 (8th Cir. 1995)
interps.summary: The court held that a child-welfare worker’s alleged failure to follow a state-court reunification plan or state agency policy did not, standing alone, establish a violation of the parent’s federal constitutional liberty interest. It affirmed qualified immunity because no clearly established constitutional right required strict adherence to the plan.
excerpts: Mr. Ebmeier claims the defendants “disregarded” both the Buffalo County Court’s order approving the reunification plan and NDSS policy, thereby violating his “constitutionally protected fundamental liberty interest in the care and custody of his children.” As the District Court put it, Mr. Ebmeier asserts a “clearly established right requiring the defendants to adhere strictly to the court order that directed them to devise a reunification plan.

It is established beyond peradventure that a state actor’s failure to observe a duty imposed by state law, standing alone, is not a sufficient foundation on which to erect a section 1983 claim. Although it is true that constitutional significance may attach to certain interests created by state law, not every transgression of state law does double duty as a constitutional violation.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Thomason v. SCAN Volunteer Services, Inc., 85 F.3d 1365 (8th Cir. 1996)
interps.summary: The court recognized that parents possess a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, but held that the interest is not absolute and is limited by the government’s compelling interest in protecting children. In the context of a child-abuse investigation, officials are entitled to qualified immunity when an otherwise disruptive action is reasonably founded on suspicion of abuse.
excerpts: Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.) (Myers) (citing Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 2991-92, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1988)), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828, 108 S.Ct. 97, 98 L.Ed.2d 58 (1987); see Lux by Lux v. Hansen, 886 F.2d 1064, 1066-67 (8th Cir.1989) (Lux); Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1983).

As we stated in Myers, “the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” 810 F.2d at 1462. Moreover, as the First Circuit has correctly noted, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations.” Watterson v. Page, 987 F.2d 1, 8 (1st Cir.1993) (Watterson).

Clearly, our precedents provide that, when a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (substantive due process)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Zakrzewski v. Fox, 87 F.3d 1011 (8th Cir. 1996)
interps.summary: The court recognized that parents have a fundamental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, but held that the interest is not absolute and that visitation rights may be subject to due-process scrutiny. It further held that a substantive due-process claim based on interference with visitation requires conduct that abuses official power and shocks the conscience; the court found no prior case establishing a constitutional violation at that level.
excerpts: It is beyond question that “ ‘[pjarents have a fundamental “liberty interest” in the care, custody, and management of their children.’ ” Fitzgerald v. Williamson, 787 F.2d 403, 407 (8th Cir.1986) (quoting Ruffalo v. Civiletti, 702 F.2d 710, 715 (8th Cir.1983), citing Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 753, 102 S.Ct. 1388, 1394, 71 L.Ed.2d 599 (1982)) (alteration in original). This right, however, is not absolute. Manzano v. South Dakota Dep’t of Social Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 510 (8th Cir.1995).

To the extent Zakrzewski claims a substantive due process violation of Ms parenting liberty interest, he must demonstrate that the defendants abused their official power in a manner that shocks the conscience, regardless of whether state-law remedies are available. New v. City of Minneapolis, 792 F.2d 724, 725-26 (8th Cir.1986). “[T]he theory of substantive due process is properly reserved for truly egregious and extraordinary cases,” Myers v. Scott County, 868 F.2d 1017, 1019 (8th Cir.1989),

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Amerson v. Iowa, 94 F.3d 510 (8th Cir. 1996)
interps.summary: The court applied Younger and related abstention principles to dismiss Amerson’s equitable claims because parallel state proceedings concerning termination of parental rights were pending. It also held that federal relief, including damages dependent on invalidating the state judgment, was impermissible in this domestic-relations context and would improperly require review of the state custody determination.
excerpts: We conclude without extended discussion that the district court’s detailed discussion of the abstention principles cited above is correct as applied to Amerson’s equitable claims, including those for injunctive relief. The relief Amerson seeks is redress for “alleged tortious interference with her parental rights.” (Appellant’s Br. at 6.) Because the state courts have terminated her parental rights, redress for this alleged interference cannot be granted without first disturbing the state court adjudication terminating her parental rights, a matter of substantial public concern.

Additionally, several state court proceedings and appeals concerning the same issues asserted here were pending at the time of the district court’s decision. See Younger, 401 U.S. at 43-54, 91 S.Ct. at 750-55 (holding that, with a few exceptions, federal courts cannot interfere with pending state court criminal proceedings). See also Ankenbrandt, 504 U.S. at 705, 112 S.Ct. at 2215-16 (noting that Younger abstention has been extended to the civil context). Thus, the district court did not err in applying these principles of abstention to Amerson’s equitable claims.

The Supreme Court has long rejected federal court interference in state domestic relations policy. See Ankenbrandt, 504 U.S. at 701-02, 112 S.Ct. at 2213-14 (noting that claims seeking to restore a child to the custody of a parent are within the subject of domestic relations, which belongs to the states); Lannan v. Maul, 979 F.2d 627, 630-31 (8th Cir.1992) (discussing Ankenbrandt and noting that the domestic relations exception is narrow and “divests federal courts of power to issue divorce, alimony decrees and child custody orders”).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Crawford, 115 F.3d 1397 (8th Cir. 1997)
interps.summary: The court held that the domestic-relations exception, which is limited to diversity cases involving divorce, alimony, and child-custody decrees, did not apply to a federal prosecution under the CSRA because jurisdiction rested on federal-question criminal jurisdiction. It also held that Younger abstention was unwarranted because the CSRA supplements, rather than interferes with, state enforcement of child-support obligations.
excerpts: Moreover, Crawford’s reliance upon the “domestic relations exception” is misplaced. In Ankenbrandt v. Richards, 504 U.S. 689, 701-04, 112 S.Ct. 2206, 2213-15, 119 L.Ed.2d 468 (1992), the Supreme Court reaffirmed the validity of the “domestic relations exception” in diversity cases, but specifically limited application of that exception to divorce and alimony decrees and child custody orders. That exception is irrelevant to federal prosecutions under the CSRA because the district courts’ jurisdiction in such cases does not rest upon diversity, but rather is based upon 18 U.S.C. § 3231 (“The district courts of the United States shall have original jurisdiction, exclusive of the courts of the States, of all offenses against the laws of the United States.

Similarly, contrary to Crawford’s argument based upon the Younger abstention doctrine, we discern no interference with the states’ abilities to apply and enforce their criminal laws. “[T]he CSRA does not displace any approach taken by the state in addressing the problem of delinquent parents but rather supplements such state initiatives by fortifying law enforcement efforts and existing state penalties.” Hampshire, 95 F.3d at 1004. In sum, the district court correctly rejected Crawford’s argument that principles of federalism and comity compel abstention. Accord Johnson, 114 F.3d at 480-82 (rejecting substantially the same arguments). We therefore hold that the district court appropriately declined to abstain.
provisions: Domestic-relations exception to diversity jurisdiction; 18 U.S.C. § 3231

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Whisman ex rel. Whisman v. Rinehart, 119 F.3d 1303 (8th Cir. 1997)
interps.summary: The court held that parents possess a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, and that parents and children have a corresponding liberty interest in familial association. The alleged removal and continued retention of the child without reasonable suspicion of abuse or a prompt post-deprivation hearing stated a due-process claim.
excerpts: Michelle has alleged that defendants’ actions violated her constitutional right to not be deprived of the custody of her son without due process of law. Parents have a recognized liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.1987). Both parents and children have a liberty interest in the care and companionship of each other.

Even if defendants had a right to take temporary custody of Joel, defendants had a corresponding obligation to afford Michelle and Joel an adequate post-deprivation hearing. Doe v. Hennepin County, 858 F.2d 1325, 1329 (8th Cir.1988). The right to an adequate post-deprivation hearing was clearly established in February of 1995.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Prudential Insurance v. Hinkel, 121 F.3d 364 (8th Cir. 1997)
interps.summary: The court applied the federal-preemption rule recognized in Ridgway, holding that state divorce decrees and related state-law property claims cannot override federally established beneficiary designations for military life-insurance benefits. It therefore concluded that Hinkel was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
excerpts: In Ridgway, Sergeant Ridgway and his first wife were divorced and he was ordered to keep in force the insurance policies on his life for the benefit of the three children of the marriage. After his remarriage, Sergeant Ridgway changed the beneficiary designation on his SGLIA policy from his first wife, April, to his second wife, Donna. Both April and Donna filed claims for the proceeds of the policy. April’s claim was on behalf of the children, pursuant to the divorce decree. The Supreme Judicial Court of Maine held that Donna must hold the policy proceeds as constructive trustee on behalf of the children. The United States Supreme Court reversed the decision of the Supreme Judicial Court of Maine. Ridgway, 454 U.S. at 63, 102 S.Ct. at 59.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Painter v. Golden Rule Insurance, 121 F.3d 436 (8th Cir. 1997)
interps.summary: The court applied ERISA conflict-preemption principles, holding that state-law claims conflicting with ERISA’s specifically prescribed benefit remedies are preempted. It distinguished this analysis from broader “relate to” preemption.
excerpts: However, some ERISA eases involve the distinct question of conflict preemption — whether a state law is preempted because it conflicts with a specific portion of the complex ERISA statute. If there is a conflict, state law is preempted, whether or not “the statutory phrase ‘relate to’ provides further and additional support for the pre-emption claim.” Boggs v. Boggs, — U.S. -, -, 117 S.Ct. 1754, 1761, 138 L.Ed.2d 45 (1997). In our view, this is a ease of conflict preemption.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Singleton v. Cecil, 133 F.3d 631 (8th Cir. 1998)
interps.summary: The court applied the fundamental right to marry under the Fourteenth Amendment. It held that the city’s termination of Singleton based on his wife’s conduct did not directly or substantially interfere with, or significantly discourage, the marriage and therefore did not violate substantive due process.
excerpts: Singleton claims that his termination violated his substantive due process right of privacy in his marital relationship. The fundamental right of privacy embodies the “principle that personal decisions that profoundly affect bodily integrity, identity, and destiny should be largely beyond the reach of government.” Planned Parenthood v. Casey, 505 U.S. 833, 927, 112 S.Ct. 2791, 2846, 120 L.Ed.2d 674 (1992) (Blackmun, J., concurring in part, concurring in the judgment in part, and dissenting in part). The Supreme Court has recognized “that the right to marry is part of the fundamental ‘right of privacy implicit in the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process clause.” Zablocki v. Redhail, 434 U.S. 374, 384, 98 S.Ct. 673, 680, 54 L.Ed.2d 618 (1977).

This right, however, does not invalidate every state action that has some impact on marriage. See Gorrie v. Bowen, 809 F.2d 508, 522-23 (8th Cir.1987) (“Not every regulation that involves or somehow regulates on the basis of family membership is unconstitutional.”). Rather, the government is free to impose “reasonable regulations that do not significantly interfere with decisions to enter into the marital relationship____” Zablocki, 434 U.S. at 386, 98 S.Ct. at 681. Government action “must interfere ‘directly and substantially5 with family choices before it is unconstitutional,” Gorrie, 809 F.2d at 523 (quoting Zablocki, 434 U.S. at 387, 98 S.Ct. at 681) (citation omitted), but action having only a collateral effect on family decisions typically does not violate that right.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Peter v. Wedl, 155 F.3d 992 (8th Cir. 1998)
interps.summary: The court recognized that parents have a constitutional liberty to choose the education their child receives, relying on Pierce and Yoder. It considered whether withholding special-education services from a child attending a private religious school impermissibly burdened or conditioned that parental choice.
excerpts: It is undisputed that Aaron has the right to receive special education services if he attends a public school. It is also clear that the Westendorps have the constitutional right to choose the education that Aaron shall receive. See Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510, 534-35, 45 S.Ct. 571, 69 L.Ed. 1070 (1925) (discussing “the liberty of parents and guardians to direct the upbringing and education of children under their control,” which “excludes any general power of the State to standardize its children by forcing them to accept instruction from public teachers only”); see also Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205, 233-34, 92 S.Ct. 1526, 32 L.Ed.2d 15 (1972).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Smith, 171 F.3d 617 (8th Cir. 1999)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and construed § 921(a)(33)'s definition of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. It addressed whether the Iowa assault conviction involved the required use or attempted use of physical force, a domestic relationship, and an informed waiver of counsel.
excerpts: Congress enacted 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) in 1996, providing: “It shall be unlawful for any person ... who has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence ... to possess in or affecting commerce, any firearm." Section 921(a)(33) (A) (ii) defines "misdemeanor crime of domestic violence" as one that "has, as an element, the use or attempted use of physical force, or the threatened use of a deadly weapon, committed by a current or former spouse, ... [or] by a person with whom the victim shares a child.

Smith challenges the application to his case of 18 U.S.C.A. § 921(a)(33), which defines a “misdemean- or crime of domestic violence,” arguing that: 1) Iowa Code § 708.1, which defines assault, does not contain the required elements of: a) the use or attempted use of physical force, and b) a domestic relationship; and 2) he did not intelligently and knowingly waive his right to counsel at the underlying plea hearing as required by § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(I).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Patterson v. United States, 181 F.3d 927 (8th Cir. 1999)
interps.summary: The court applied the QTIP marital-deduction provisions to determine whether the property passing to the marital trust qualified for the deduction. It explained that qualification requires passage of the property from the decedent to the spouse, a qualifying income interest for life, and a timely election, including the restriction on appointing property to anyone other than the surviving spouse.
excerpts: In order to qualify for QTIP deductibility, property must pass from the decedent to the spouse, the spouse must have a qualifying income .interest for life, and an election must be made on the tax return. 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(i). A qualifying income for life is one in which “no person has a power to appoint any part of the property to any person other than the surviving spouse.” Id. at § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Sabhari v. Reno, 197 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 1999)
interps.summary: The court held that a United States citizen may petition to classify an alien spouse as an immediate relative under 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i), but that the petition must be denied under § 1154(c) when the marriage was entered into to evade the immigration laws. The court upheld review of the agency decision and addressed whether substantial evidence supported the marriage-fraud determination.
excerpts: When a United States citizen marries an alien, the citizen may petition the INS to have his or her spouse classified as an immediate relative. See 8 U.S.C. § 1154 (establishing petitioning procedure) and § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i) (defining immediate relative to include citizen’s spouse). Once so classified, the alien may then apply under a separate procedure for an adjustment of immigration status — a process which will upgrade the alien to the status of lawful permanent resident of the United States.

Approval of the alien’s petition for adjustment of status is not a foregone conclusion, however, and it has long been recognized that the INS may combat fraud by refusing to confer benefits where a marriage has been entered so as to circumvent the immigration laws. See Lutwak v. United States, 344 U.S. 604, 73 S.Ct. 481, 97 L.Ed. 593 (1953); 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c)(1994) (“no petition shall be approved ... by reason of a marriage determined by the Attorney General to have been entered into for the purpose of evading the immigration laws,

norms.b_justification: Sabhari interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c), including its prohibition on approving a petition based on a marriage determined to have been entered into to evade the immigration laws. The listed post-decision amendments do not alter subsection (c), so the interpreted language remains identical in wording and function, although it is not reproduced in the supplied current-text excerpt.

Sabhari interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i)’s definition of an immediate relative to include the spouse of a United States citizen, together with the anti-fraud provision in § 1154(c). The later 2000 and 2009 amendments changed other language in § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i), but did not alter the spouse-definition language applied in the decision, so its wording and function remain consistent.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Taylor v. United States, 212 F.3d 395 (8th Cir. 2000)
interps.summary: The court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision protects a qualified pension from creditor reach but does not prevent the pension from being treated as disposable income in calculating a Chapter 13 repayment plan. The court distinguished Patterson v. Shumate, which concerned the bankruptcy estate’s property under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).
excerpts: The Taylors argue that ERISA’s anti-alienation provisions, see 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), exempts the pension plan from the disposable income calculation. The Taylors base their argument on Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753, 112 S.Ct. 2242, 119 L.Ed.2d 519 (1992). In Patterson, the Supreme Court held that ERISA’s anti-alienation provision constituted an enforceable transfer restriction in a proceeding instituted under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).

The fact that a pension is exempt from the reach of creditors does not preclude a bankruptcy court from finding that the pension is also disposable income for purposes of Chapter 13. The question of whether income from a pension is exempt

norms.b_justification: Taylor interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation requirement in 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1). The post-decision amendments identified affect only § 1056(d)(3)(B), not subsection (d)(1), whose wording and function remain unchanged; however, the supplied excerpts do not quote the interpreted language verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Hutzell, 217 F.3d 966 (8th Cir. 2000)
interps.summary: The court held that a prosecution under § 922(g)(9), enforced through § 924(a)(2), requires knowledge of the facts constituting the offense, but not knowledge that firearm possession was unlawful. It also held that applying § 922(g)(9) to a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor domestic-violence offense did not violate due process for lack of notice.
excerpts: The government asserts that 18 U.S.C. § 924(a)(2), which provides the penalties for those who “knowingly” violate § 922(g), requires it to prove only that Mr. Hutzell knew of the facts constituting the offense, not that he knew that it was illegal for him to possess a gun. We can find no fault with the government’s proposed construction of the statute. See Bryan v. United States, 524 U.S. 184, 192-93, 118 S.Ct. 1939, 141 L.Ed.2d 197 (1998). As we held in United States v. Farrell, 69 F.3d 891, 893 (8th Cir.1995), cert. denied, 516 U.S. 1181, 116 S.Ct. 1283, 134 L.Ed.2d 228 (1996), § 924(a)(2) does not “require knowledge of the law nor an intent to violate it.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Lewis, 236 F.3d 948 (8th Cir. 2001)
interps.summary: The court upheld 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) against an equal-protection challenge, holding that Congress could rationally prohibit firearm possession by persons convicted of misdemeanor domestic-violence offenses. The court also relied on the statutory civil-rights-restoration exception in § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii) and its earlier treatment of that provision.
excerpts: Under Section 922(g)(9), a person convicted of a domestic-violence misdemeanor loses the right to carry a gun, while people convicted of other misdemeanors do not. The two groups, as defendant argues, are differently treated, but we cannot agree that the difference is sufficiently arbitrary to violate due process.’ One might think that other misdemeanors are just as serious as domestic-violence misdemeanors, but this is the sort of judgment that must be made by legislators, not judges.

An analogous case is United States v. Smith, 171 F.3d 617, 623-26 (8th Cir.1999). Smith involved Section 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), which provides an exception to the prohibition of Section 922(g)(9) if the person convicted of a domestic-violence misdemeanor has had his civil rights restored. In Smith, the defendant had been convicted of a domestic-violence misdemeanor in Iowa, but had never lost his civil rights, because civil rights are not stripped from individuals convicted of misdemeanors in Iowa.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), concerning the exception where civil rights have been restored. That provision was not amended after the 2001 decision and remains identical in wording and function; later amendments affected other portions of § 921(a)(33).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Keeney, 241 F.3d 1040 (8th Cir. 2001)
interps.summary: The court construed the civil-rights-restoration exception to the federal prohibition on firearm possession by persons convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence. It held that the district court misconstrued the exception and reversed dismissal of the indictment under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9).
excerpts: For reversal, the government argues that the district court misconstrued the so-called civil rights restoration exception of 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a)(33)(B)(ii) in reaching its decision to dismiss Keeney’s indictment. For the reasons stated below, we reverse the district court’s decision to dismiss Keeney’s indictment and remand this matter to the district court for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Section 922(a)(6) prohibits any person from knowingly making false or fictitious statements in connection with the acquisition or attempted acquisition of a firearm. Section 922(g)(9) prohibits persons convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence from possessing a firearm. Both offenses were predicated on Keeney’s prior conviction for a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under North Dakota law. Keeney moved to dismiss the indictment pursuant to the so-called civil rights restoration exception, which provides:

norms.b_justification: United States v. Keeney interpreted the civil-rights-restoration exception in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii). Although the supplied excerpts do not reproduce the interpreted language verbatim, no later amendment affected subparagraph (B)(ii), and its current restoration/expungement/pardon rule remains substantively the same.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Vaughn v. Ruoff, 253 F.3d 1124 (8th Cir. 2001)
interps.summary: The court applied Fourteenth Amendment due process principles to parents’ claims that a state social worker conditioned reunification with their children on sterilization. It treated the alleged interference with the Vaughns’ parental and familial interests as a constitutional deprivation relevant to qualified-immunity analysis.
excerpts: till in the hospital, Ruoff told Margaret that if she got her “tubes tied, that [she] would have [her] kids back in two to three weeks.” Ruoff also told both Margaret and Kevin Sr. that “if [he] or [Margaret] would get sterilized, [their] chances of getting the kids back would be really great.” Margaret then agreed to a tubal ligation, and Ruoff scheduled the procedure for October 8, 1994.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND APPLICATION TO FACTS Ruoff argues that she is entitled to qualified immunity on the Vaughns’ due process claims. Qualified immunity analysis initially asks the following two questions: (1) was there a deprivation of a constitutional right, and, if so, (2) was the right clearly established at the time of the deprivation? County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833, 841 n. 5, 118 S.Ct. 1708, 140 L.Ed.2d 1043 (1998). If either question is answered in the negative, the public official is entitled to qualified immunity.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Silverman v. Silverman, 267 F.3d 788 (8th Cir. 2001)
interps.summary: The court held that Younger abstention principles did not permit outright dismissal of a Hague Convention return petition because Article 12 makes return relief non-discretionary once wrongful removal or retention is established. Although state custody proceedings were pending, the proper course was to remand for determination of whether the children were wrongfully removed.
excerpts: Younger abstention prohibits a federal court from interfering in pending state civil cases where (1) there is an ongoing state proceeding (2) that implicates important state interests and (3) there is an adequate opportunity in the state proceeding to raise the federal issues.

In the absence of discretion with respect to relief, abstention principles do not permit an outright dismissal of a Hague petition. See Yamaha Motor Corp., U.S.A. v. Stroud, 179 F.3d 598, 603-04 (8th Cir.1999).

Because the Hague issue has not been addressed, we believe the appropriate course of action is to remand the matter to the district court to consider whether the Silverman children were wrongfully removed.
provisions: Younger abstention: ongoing state proceeding, important state interest, and adequate opportunity to raise federal issues

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Gipson v. Immigration & Naturalization Service, 284 F.3d 913 (8th Cir. 2002)
interps.summary: The court held that classification of an alien spouse as an immediate relative is discretionary and may be denied when the agency lacks reliable information about the applicant’s identity, origin, and family ties. A valid marriage license alone does not require approval of the immediate-relative petition.
excerpts: Decisions whether to grant preferential immigration classification are within the discretion of the INS, acting as an arm of the attorney general. 8 U.S.C. § 1154(a)(1)(H); Choi v. INS, 798 F.2d 1189, 1191 (8th Cir.1986) (reviewing decision denying non-immigrant treaty investor status); see also Egan v. Weiss, 119 F.3d 106, 107 (2d Cir.1997) (per curiam) (reviewing denial of petition to have alien classified as spouse); North American Industries, Inc. v. Feldman, 722 F.2d 893, 898 (1st Cir.1983) (reviewing denial of petition to have alien classified as sixth-preference -immigrant on basis of profession).

A United States citizen can petition to have an alien spouse classified as an “immediate relative,” a preferential immigration classification. 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i). Immediate relatives may be admitted to the United States without numerical limitations. 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b). Once an alien’s petition for identification as an immediate relative is approved, he or she may then petition for an adjustment of status to that of a person admitted for permanent residence. 8 C.F.R. § 245 et seq. Sathekge argues that the fact of his valid marriage license is enough to carry him through step one and that the BIA denial of his reclassification as an immediate relative therefore constituted an abuse of discretion.

As appellees point out, there can be no meaningful review of the truth behind a petition for classification as an immediate relative if the reviewing agency does not have accurate information regarding the name, place of origin, and family ties of the applicant. Based on the inconsistent data given by Sathekge, the INS could not even determin

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i) insofar as a U.S. citizen’s spouse may qualify as an “immediate relative,” and addressed the agency’s discretion in evaluating that classification. The 2009 amendment altered only the separate surviving-spouse provision in the second sentence of clause (i), not the spouse definition applied in Gipson, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Gainey v. Barnhart, 299 F.3d 1004 (8th Cir. 2002)
interps.summary: The court applied the Social Security widow’s-benefits provisions requiring the claimant to qualify as the insured wage earner’s widow under applicable state law. It held that the claimant could not qualify through a common-law marriage because two prior undissolved marriages created a legal impediment to that marriage.
excerpts: Geraldine Gainey (“Geraldine”) appeals from the district court’s affirmance of a final decision of the Commissioner of Social Security Administration (“Commissioner”) denying her claim for social security widow’s benefits under 42 U.S.C. § 402(e) of the Social Security Act. The central issue in this case is whether Geraldine can be considered the widow of deceased wage earner Everett Leach (“Leach”) by virtue of a common-law marriage due to the legal impediment of two prior undissolved marriages.

To receive widow’s benefits, Geraldine must demonstrate that she is the widow of the insured wage earner based on the laws of the state where the insured had a permanent home at the time of his death. See 20 C.F.R. § 404.345. Moreover, because Geraldine and Leach never had a formal marriage ceremony, under federal regulations, Geraldine must demonstrate

norms.b_justification: The decision construed the widow-status requirement under 42 U.S.C. § 402(e), in conjunction with § 416(h)(1)(A), concerning recognition of a common-law marriage under applicable state law. The later amendments identified affect benefit-computation provisions in § 402(e)(2), not the widow-definition or state-law-marriage provisions applied in Gainey, so the interpreted language remains functionally identical.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Hogan v. Raytheon, Co., 302 F.3d 854 (8th Cir. 2002)
interps.summary: The court held that a domestic relations order may be qualified posthumously when the plan receives notice of the divorce decree and the subsequent order qualifying the decree is filed within ERISA’s eighteen-month period. The March 9, 1998 order therefore satisfied the QDRO requirements and entitled the former spouse to surviving-spouse benefits.
excerpts: Second, Raytheon argues that the district court erred in finding that a domestic relations order can be qualified posthumously. We disagree. The district court correctly held that the March 9,1998 Order meets the requirements of a QDRO because Raytheon was put on notice that the Decree had issued and may be a QDRO, and the March 9, 1998 Order was filed during the eighteen-month period permitted under ERISA to secure a QDRO. See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(H) (1994); Trs. of the Dirs. Guild of Am. Producer Pension Benefits Plans v. Tise, 234 F.3d 415 (9th Cir.2000).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(H), concerning the treatment of a domestic-relations order filed within the statutory 18-month period after a participant’s death. The listed 2022 amendments amended only § 1056(d)(3)(B), including the addition of Tribal domestic-relations laws, and did not alter subsection (H); thus the interpreted rule remains identical in function, although the quoted language is not reproduced verbatim in the supplied current-text excerpt.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Silverman v. Silverman, 312 F.3d 914 (8th Cir. 2002)
interps.summary: The court held that habitual residence under the Hague Convention and ICARA is a purely factual, case-specific inquiry, reviewed for clear error. The parent seeking return bears the preponderance-of-the-evidence burden to show that the children were removed from their habitual residence; because the children’s habitual residence was the United States, the court did not reach the Article 13(b) defense.
excerpts: habitual residence” has not been defined in either the Convention or the Act, and courts must look to the legislative history for guidance on the matter. The official history and commentary in the Federal Register explains that “ ‘habitual residence’ ... is, in fact, a familiar notion of the Hague Conference, where it is understood as a ;purely factual concept, to be differentiated especially from that of the ‘domicile.

In its conclusions of law, the district court found that the determination of habitual residence is a fact-based inquiry to be analyzed on a case-by-case basis. We agree with the court below that the Silverman children’s habitual residence is solely a question of fact, and we therefore review the district court’s holding for clear error.

Pursuant to the Hague Convention, Robert Silverman (Robert) must initially prove by a preponderance of the evidence that Julie Silverman (Julie) removed their children from their habitual residence, which Robert alleges is Israel. 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).

norms.b_justification: Silverman interpreted Hague Convention Article 3 and 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A), holding that habitual residence is a fact-based, case-by-case inquiry. That approach is consistent in wording and function with Monasky’s current totality-of-the-circumstances rule, even though the quoted language does not appear verbatim in the current text.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Wilson, 315 F.3d 972 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied its binding precedent upholding the constitutionality of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), which prohibits firearm possession by individuals subject to qualifying restraining orders. It affirmed the denial of Wilson’s motion to dismiss.
excerpts: Wilson admittedly seeks reversal of clearly established precedent. We decline to do so and affirm the District Court’s decision to deny his motion to dismiss. . The Honorable E. Richard Webber, United States District Court Judge for the Eastern District of Missouri. . Wilson relies heavily upon United States v. Emerson, 270 F.3d 203, 259 (5th Cir.2001) (holding that the Second Amendment "protects the right of individuals, including those not then actually a member of any militia or engaged in active military service or training, to privately possess and bear their own firearms....”). However, Emerson nonetheless upheld the constitutionality of § 922(g)(8) which prohibits an individual subject to certain restraining orders from possessing a firearm.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Nelson v. Ramette, 322 F.3d 541 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The court held that an alternate payee’s pending distribution under a qualified domestic relations order is an interest protected by ERISA’s anti-alienation provision. Because a QDRO grants the alternate payee beneficiary status, the interest was excluded from the debtor’s bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2).
excerpts: Ronald claimed in the bankruptcy proceeding that his pending distribution from the retirement plan should be excluded from his bankruptcy estate pursuant to 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2) because it was subject to ERISA’s anti-alienation provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1).

The BAP reversed, holding the plain language of ERISA grants beneficiary status to alternate payees under a QDRO, and therefore entitles those persons to the protection of ERISA’s anti-alienation provision. Nelson, 274 B.R. at 798. The BAP relied upon two Supreme Court decisions, Patterson v. Shumate, 504 U.S. 753, 760, 112 S.Ct. 2242, 119 L.Ed.2d 519 (1992) (holding that a debtor’s interest in an ERISA-quali-fied plan was excluded from bankruptcy estate pursuant to ERISA’s anti-alienation provision and 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2)), and Boggs v. Boggs, 520 U.S. 833, 846-47, 117 S.Ct. 1754, 138 L.Ed.2d 45 (1997) (generally recognizing that QDROs confer beneficiary status upon certain nonparticipants and give those persons the same protection under ERISA as plan participants).

norms.b_justification: Nelson interpreted ERISA’s anti-alienation provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1), and the QDRO provisions recognizing alternate payees as beneficiaries protected under ERISA. The 2022 amendments affected § 1056(d)(3)(B)’s domestic-relations-order definition by adding Tribal-law language and related concluding provisions, but did not substantively alter § 1056(d)(1) or the QDRO/alternate-payee language relevant to Nelson’s holding.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Ballinger v. Culotta, 322 F.3d 546 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that Rooker-Feldman barred Ballinger’s § 1983 claims because they challenged a state-court custody judgment and could succeed only if the state court had wrongly decided the custody issues. The federal action would therefore operate as a prohibited appellate review of the state judgment.
excerpts: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine provides that, “with the exception of habe-as corpus petitions, lower federal courts lack subject matter jurisdiction over challenges to state court judgments.” Lemonds v. St. Louis County, 222 F.3d 488, 492 (8th Cir.2000) (citing Feldman, 460 U.S. at 476, 103 S.Ct. 1303; Rooker, 263 U.S. at 416, 44 S.Ct. 149). District courts may not review state court decisions, “even if those challenges allege that the state court’s action was unconstitutional,”

A claim brought in federal court is inextricably intertwined with a state court judgment “if the federal claim succeeds only to the extent that the state court wrongly decided the issue before it.” Id. at 493 (citing Pennzoil Co. v. Texaco, Inc., 481 U.S. 1, 25, 107 S.Ct. 1519, 95 L.Ed.2d 1 (1987) (Marshall, J., concurring)). Balling-er alleged in the complaint that Judge Pratt of the Circuit Court of Clay County violated Missouri law by awarding custody of John Ballinger to the Rheeses, who neither had “intervened in the action, nor filed a motion to modify.

Because “the relief requested in [Ballinger’s] federal [§ 1983] action would effectively reverse the state court decision or void its ruling,” Bechtold v. City of Rosemount, 104 F.3d 1062, 1065 (8th Cir.1997), the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars the district court from considering Balling-er’s claims, as the federal court action would amount to a “prohibited appeal of the state-court judgment,” id. at 1066 (citation omitted).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle, 335 F.3d 684 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The court applied the Rooker-Feldman doctrine in the context of a federal challenge involving state child-protection proceedings. It explained that a losing state-court party may not obtain de facto appellate review of a state judgment in federal district court, but indicated that Heartland’s request for injunctive relief was not necessarily barred because it did not interfere with the state-court judgment.
excerpts: On appeal from this order, Waddle first maintains that the District Court should have abstained from exercising jurisdiction over Heartland’s claim for preliminary in-junctive relief. He argues that the federal court is being asked to interfere with his responsibility to enforce the State’s child protection laws, and the District Court therefore should have abstained from hearing Heartland’s claims.

Under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, “a party losing in state court is barred from seeking what in substance would be appellate review of the state judgment in a United States district court, based on the losing party’s claim that the state judgment itself violates the loser’s federal rights.” Johnson v. De Grandy, 512 U.S. 997, 1005-06, 114 S.Ct. 2647, 129 L.Ed.2d 775 (1994). In other words, original federal jurisdiction over state-court judgments is reserved to the Supreme Court. Verizon Md. Inc. v. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 535 U.S. 635, 644 n. 3, 122 S.Ct. 1753, 152 L.Ed.2d 871 (2002).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Taylor, 338 F.3d 947 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The court held that the divorce order became a qualified domestic relations order when the plan administrator approved the corrected order within ERISA’s eighteen-month period, and that Mary’s interest related back to the original domestic relations order. The court also held that ERISA preempted reliance on Texas community-property law and state-law perfection requirements.
excerpts: In this case, Northwest determined, within eighteen months of the date the first payment would have been made under the DRO, that the DRO, as modified, was a QDRO. Thus, Mary satisfied ERISA’s requirements for alienating pension plan proceeds. Requiring Mary to satisfy state law perfection requirements would conflict with ERISA’s policy of ensuring that plan sponsors are subject to a uniform body of law.

Our holdings in Nelson and here, recognizing the DRO establishes a “direct interest in plan funds,” and upon qualification, the interest relates back to the initial DRO date, further the statutory scheme to protect employee retirement benefits for beneficiaries of the plans, including divorced spouses.

As a legal matter, when the DRO issued, Francis was no longer the owner of 90 percent of the Northwest ERISA plans. Mary was awarded this share as part of the divorce. Mary, the property, and the amount were identified clearly, only the details of qualification remained to transform the DRO into a QDRO.
