norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3), particularly subsection (d)(3)(H), concerning the plan administrator’s qualification of a domestic relations order and the relation-back of a later QDRO determination. The listed post-decision amendments affect only § 1056(d)(3)(B), adding Tribal domestic-relations-law language, and do not alter the interpreted provision’s wording or function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Silverman v. Silverman, 338 F.3d 886 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that the children’s habitual residence was Israel and that returning them there did not create a grave risk of harm under Article 13(b) of the Hague Convention as implemented by ICARA. It also held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar the federal Hague proceeding because the state court had not decided the Convention-specific issues of habitual residence or wrongful removal and retention.
excerpts: Because we find that the children’s habitual residence was Israel at the time of their removal and that there is no grave risk of harm to the children if they are returned to Israel, we reverse the district court.

The state court determined neither the “habitual residence” of the children nor the issue of “wrongful removal or retention” as required by and defined in the Hague Convention and ICARA. Indeed, it was not asked to do so.

norms.b_justification: Silverman interpreted Hague Convention article 3 and ICARA’s wrongful-removal provisions, including the child’s habitual residence, through a fact-intensive assessment of the circumstances. Its application is functionally consistent with Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances rule; the later formulation does not materially alter the habitual-residence inquiry.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Swipies v. Kofka, 348 F.3d 701 (8th Cir. 2003)
interps.summary: The court held that parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, including a right not to be separated from a child based only on an officer’s suspicion that another person might abuse the child. It concluded that the alleged removal would violate that parental liberty interest and affirmed denial of qualified-immunity summary judgment because material facts were disputed.
excerpts: Parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children. See Manzano, 60 F.3d at 509. This interest can be limited by the state’s compelling interest in protecting a child: “the parental liberty interest in keeping the family unit intact is not a clearly established right in the context of reasonable suspicion that parents may be abusing children.

Viewing the facts here in the light most favorable to Mr. Swipies, and noting the inconsistencies among Deputy Kofka’s statements in the summary judgment record, we conclude that Mr. Swipies retained the right not to be separated from his child in the face of Deputy Kofka’s suspicion that Mr. Stark might abuse Kendra. We further conclude that it would have been clear to a reasonable officer that removing Kendra in those circumstances would violate Mr. Swipies’s parental liberty interest.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Cuervo, 354 F.3d 969 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) and the definition of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence in § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) to a defendant convicted of assaulting a long-term extramarital partner. It affirmed the firearm convictions, rejecting the defendant’s as-applied vagueness challenge.
excerpts: Under § 922(g)(9), it is unlawful for a person who has been convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence to possess a firearm. A crime of domestic violence is defined as one which involves the use or threatened use of physical force or a deadly weapon “by a person who is cohabitating with or has cohabitated with the victim as a spouse” or “by a person similarly situated to a spouse ... of the victim.” 18 U.S.C. § 921 (a)(33)(A)(ii).

Schoenauer had previously been convicted of assaulting his secretary, whom he had engaged in a long-term extramarital affair. The evidence showed that she and Schoenauer stayed together periodically at an apartment Schoenauer kept. During this time, Schoenauer remained married and lived with his wife.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), particularly the categories covering a person who is cohabiting with or has cohabited with the victim as a spouse and a person similarly situated to a spouse. Although the 2022 amendment removed the conjunction before the latter category and added a separate dating-relationship category, it did not change the wording or function of the relationship categories applied in Cuervo.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Al Khouri v. Ashcroft, 362 F.3d 461 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court applied procedural due process principles to a family-based immigration proceeding. It held that an immigration judge’s failure to adequately explain hearing procedures and elicit pertinent facts can constitute fundamental error, and that prejudice does not require but-for causation when the error may have prevented the alien from presenting relevant evidence.
excerpts: Given that the fundamental error in Mr. A1 Khouri’s hearing prevented him from fully developing the merits of his case, we cannot say that, but for the lack of process afforded him, he would have been granted relief from removal. Prejudice in this context, however, does not require “but for” causation.

Prejudice in this context, however, does not require “but for” causation. Instead, “prejudice may be shown where the IJ’s inadequate explanation of the hearing procedures and failure to elicit pertinent facts prevented the alien from presenting evidence relevant to their [sic] claim.” Agyeman, 296 F.3d at 884-85.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Burton v. Richmond, 370 F.3d 723 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court applied the substantive-due-process conscience-shocking standard to claims arising from state child-welfare placement decisions. It held that the defendants’ failure to investigate abuse reports and failure to conduct a background check or home study were not sufficiently egregious to violate the plaintiffs’ substantive due process rights.
excerpts: The conduct at issue in this case consists in part of defendants’ failure to respond to two reports of sexual abuse and Allen’s failure to conduct a background check of the Huffmans prior .to the placement of plaintiffs with them. Each defendant received only a single and isolated complaint of possible sexual abuse in the Huffman home. The complaints were made by Shirley, the mother who previously had abandoned plaintiffs and who was attempting to reassert her parental rights. In these circumstances, defendants’ failure to investigate is not so outrageous or egregious as to shock the conscience and thus the failure to investigate did not violate plaintiffs’ substantive due process rights.

Similarly, Allen’s failure to conduct a home study prior to the court-ordered placement did not violate plaintiffs’ substantive due process rights. The juvenile court never ordered DFS to conduct such a study prior to placing the children in the custody of Rhonda and Jean as requested by the family. provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Substantive Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Pfeifer, 371 F.3d 430 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court affirmed Pfeifer’s conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) for possessing a firearm after a misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. It addressed the statutory requirement in § 921(a)(33)(B) concerning waiver of counsel in the predicate conviction and rejected Pfeifer’s constitutional challenges, including vagueness and Second Amendment arguments.
excerpts: Robert Lee Pfeifer conditionally pleaded guilty to possessing a firearm after being convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). Pfeifer appeals his conviction on the following statutory and constitutional grounds: 1) he did not knowingly and intelligently waive the right to counsel in the predicate domestic violence conviction, as required by 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B) in order to obtain a conviction under § 922(g)(9);

2) as applied to him, § 922(g)(9) - violates the Ex Post Facto Clause of the United States Constitution because it effectively increases the punishment for an earlier conviction; 3) § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutionally vague because it does not provide fair warning that his possession of a firearm is prohibited conduct; 4) § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutionally overreaching in that it interferes with his Second Amendment right to bear arms. We affirm.

norms.b_justification: Pfeifer interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B), particularly § 921(a)(33)(B)(i)(I)’s requirement that a defendant was represented by counsel or knowingly and intelligently waived counsel before the conviction qualifies under § 922(g)(9). That provision was not substantively amended after the decision; the later amendments affected other portions of § 921(a)(33), so the interpreted language remains identical in wording and function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Reutter ex rel. Reutter v. Barnhart, 372 F.3d 946 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court considered and rejected the claim that § 402(d)(4) violates the equal-protection component of the Fifth Amendment by disadvantaging children of female stepparents. The provision’s support requirement was applied in determining eligibility for Social Security child’s insurance benefits.
excerpts: Larry Reutter sought Social Security benefits for his daughter Destiny after the death of his wife, Ann Carlson. An administrative law judge (AL J) denied the claim, finding that Carlson had neither contributed half of Destiny’s support nor equitably adopted her, and the Appeals Council denied review. Reutter then filed this action seeking judicial review, and the district court concluded that Destiny was entitled to child’s insurance benefits but rejected the claim that the Social Security Act unconstitutionally discriminates on the basis of gender. Both parties appeal, and we affirm in part and reverse in part.

On his cross appeal Reutter contends that 42 U.S.C. § 402(d)(4) violates the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment due process clause by discriminating against the stepchildren of women. Reutter points to census data which demonstrate that men continue to earn more money than women and to studies which show that women do more unpaid housework than men. See Katherine Silbaugh, Turning Labor into Love: Housework and the Law, 91 Nw. U.L.Rev. 1 (1996).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Paracelsus Healthcare Corp. v. Philips Medical Systems, Nederland, B.V., 384 F.3d 492 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court applied the Hague Service Convention’s Central Authority procedure in determining when service on the Dutch defendant occurred. It treated transmission and receipt of the documents by the Central Authority as distinct from completed service on the defendant.
excerpts: On November 6, 2001, Paracelsus forwarded a copy of its amended complaint to Legal Language Services (LLS), a company specializing in service of process on foreign defendants in accordance with the Hague Convention. Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters, 20 U.S.T. 361, T.I.A.S. No. 6638. LLS translated the amended complaint into Dutch and prepared the additional documents needed to effect service under the Hague Convention. On November 30, 2001', LLS forwarded the completed documents to Paracelsus’s attorney for his signature. Counsel returned the documents to LLS, which in turn forwarded them to the Central Authority. The amended complaint and related documents were received by the Central Authority December 12, 2001 — one month prior to expiration of the statute of limitations. The amended complaint was not, however, served on Philips Medical until February 5, 2002.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Appleby, 380 F.3d 365 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court treated Appleby as a prohibited person under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8) and (9) when applying the firearms sentencing guideline. His prohibited-person status supported the district court’s use of the guideline’s base offense level, even though he cancelled the firearm order and never acquired the firearm.
excerpts: The guidelines provide that U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1 applies to all violations of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a). See U.S.S.G.App. A. Appleby is a “prohibited person” as defined in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8) and (9). Therefore, at sentencing, the district court determined that Appleby’s base offense level is 14. See § 2K2.1(a)(6) & comment, (n.6).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Kirchoff, 387 F.3d 748 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court held that § 922(g)(9) applied because Kirchoff had been convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. Under § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), the restoration-of-rights exception was unavailable because he had not lost his civil rights under Missouri law and therefore could not have had them restored.
excerpts: In this case, the language of Mo.Rev.Stat. § 561.026 is plain. A convicted person only loses his or her civil rights “while confined under a sentence of imprisonment.” Mo.Rev.Stat. § 561.026 (emphasis added). At the time Kirchoff committed the § 922(g) offense he was not “confined under a sentence of imprisonment” and thus had not lost his civil rights under Missouri law. As in Smith and Keeney, because Kirchoff had not lost his civil rights, under the plain language of § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), he could not have had them restored.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii), specifically the requirement that civil rights must have been lost under applicable law before they can be considered restored. That provision was not substantively amended after the decision, and its current wording and function remain identical; later amendments affected other portions of § 921(a)(33).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: De Brenner v. Ashcroft, 388 F.3d 629 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court applied the INA’s definition of “child,” including the requirement that the person be under twenty-one, in determining derivative asylum eligibility. It concluded that Romina remained eligible because she was still younger than twenty-one.
excerpts: Under the Immigration and Nationality Act, "[a] spouse or child ... of an alien who is granted asylum ... may, if not otherwise eligible for asylum ... be granted the same status as the alien if accompanying, or following to join, such alien.” 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3)(A). For the purposes of that section, a child is, inter alia, a person under twenty-one years old. 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1). Classification as a child continues if the person remains unmarried, was a child when his or her parent filed for asylum, and reached the age of twenty-one while the application was pending. 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(3)(B). Romina is still younger-than twenty-one.

norms.b_justification: The decision addressed the definition of “child” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1), particularly the requirement that the person be unmarried and under twenty-one. The relevant introductory language of § 1101(b)(1) remains substantively unchanged; the later amendments affected adoption provisions in subparagraphs (E), (F), and (G), not the language interpreted in De Brenner.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Walters v. Weiss, 392 F.3d 306 (8th Cir. 2004)
interps.summary: The court affirmed judgment against custodial parents who claimed that Arkansas’s child-support distribution practices violated Title IV-D and the Fourteenth Amendment. It upheld the conclusion that §§ 654(27) and 654B do not create an individually enforceable federal right to distribution of support payments within two business days.
excerpts: The district court held that 42 U.S.C. §§ 654(27) and 654B do not create an individually-enforceable federal right to have child support payments distributed within two business days. Id. at 1163-66 (citing Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329, 117 S.Ct. 1353, 137 L.Ed.2d 569 (1997) (Blessing

norms.b_justification: Walters v. Weiss interpreted 42 U.S.C. § 654(27), § 654B, § 654(5), and § 657 concerning distribution of child-support collections and whether those provisions create an individually enforceable right to distribution within two business days. The listed post-decision amendments do not substantively alter those interpreted provisions; the absence of a verbatim quotation requires functional rather than text-identical review.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: North American Coal Corp. Retirement Savings Plan v. Roth, 395 F.3d 916 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court applied ERISA’s QDRO provisions to uphold a plan fiduciary’s action concerning the segregation of benefits while a former spouse obtained a qualified domestic relations order. It recognized the applicable eighteen-month period for securing the QDRO and held that the former spouse’s QDRO was timely.
excerpts: Specifically, the lawsuit involved a plan fiduciary seeking to enforce plan terms and ERISA provisions regarding the segregation of plan funds while a former spouse secures a qualified domestic relations order (QDRO). See 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(G)-(H); Hogan v. Raytheon Co., 302 F.3d 854, 857 (8th Cir.2002) (recognizing 18-month period under ERISA to secure QDRO).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(G)-(H), governing QDRO determination procedures and the segregation of benefits during the applicable determination period. The listed post-decision amendments affected only subsection (d)(3)(B), not subparagraphs (G)-(H), so the interpreted language remains substantively identical in wording and function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Taylor v. Barnhart, 399 F.3d 891 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court treated Taylor’s admission as an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen under 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b) as potentially establishing a basis for lawful presence and Social Security eligibility. It held that the record was insufficient to determine whether her immediate-relative petition remained valid or was later converted, so mandamus relief was unavailable.
excerpts: This definition of an alien “lawfully present in the United States” provides a potential avenue of relief for Taylor. Taylor was inspected and admitted to the United States in 1984 as an immediate relative of a citizen of the United States. See 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b). The district court thought that her adoptive father’s petition for immediate relative status was automatically revoked when Taylor reached age 21, pursuant to 8 C.F.R. § 205.1(a)(3)(i)(F), but the record does not appear to support that conclusion.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1151(b)(2), particularly the definition of an “immediate relative” and the treatment of a child admitted on that basis. The 2009 amendment removed a two-year marriage-duration requirement applicable to surviving spouses in § 1151(b)(2)(A)(i), not the child/immediate-relative language relevant to Taylor, so the interpreted rule remains functionally identical.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Terry, 400 F.3d 575 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court affirmed Terry’s conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) for possessing a firearm after a misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. In evaluating the suppression motion, it applied § 922(g)(8), recognizing that a person subject to a qualifying protection order is generally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition and that officers could rely on collective knowledge concerning the order.
excerpts: Randy Terry entered a conditional plea of guilty to possessing a firearm after previously being convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). He did so after the district court denied his motion to suppress a firearm and ammunition seized from his vehicle and statements that he made the day following his seizure.

The defendant argues that the incriminating nature of the ammunition could not have been immediately apparent to Officer Hawk because the officer did not know of the protection order at the time that he noticed the ammunition. (A person subject to a protection order is generally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition. See 18 U.S.C. 922(g)(8).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Doe v. Miller, 405 F.3d 700 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court held that Iowa’s residency restriction for certain convicted sex offenders did not implicate a fundamental constitutional right involving family choice or family living arrangements. Because the statute did not operate directly on the family relationship, strict scrutiny was unwarranted, and the restriction did not violate substantive or procedural due process.
excerpts: The Does first invoke “the right to personal choice regarding the family.” They cite the Supreme Court’s statement in Roberts v. United States Jaycees, 468 U.S. 609, 617-18, 104 S.Ct. 3244, 82 L.Ed.2d 462 (1984), that “certain intimate human relationships must be secured against undue intrusion by the State because of the role of such relationships in safeguarding the individual freedom that is central to our constitutional scheme,” and the Court’s discussion of “marital privacy” in Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479, 485-86, 85 S.Ct. 1678, 14 L.Ed.2d 510 (1965).

We do not believe that the residency restriction of § 692A.2A implicates any fundamental right of the Does that would trigger strict scrutiny of the statute. In evaluating this argument, it is important to consider the Supreme Court’s admonition that “ ‘[sjubstantive due process’ analysis must begin with a careful description of the asserted right, for ‘[t]he doctrine of judicial self-restraint requires us to exercise the utmost care whenever we are asked to break new ground in this field.’ ” Flores, 507 U.S. at 302, 113 S.Ct. 1439 (quoting Collins v. Harker Heights, 503 U.S. 115, 125, 112 S.Ct. 1061, 117 L.Ed.2d 261 (1992)).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Townsend, 408 F.3d 1020 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) to Townsend’s guilty plea for possessing firearms after a misdemeanor conviction for a crime of domestic violence. The appeal concerned sentencing treatment of a prior burglary conviction, and the court affirmed.
excerpts: Dijuane Shante Townsend (Townsend) pled guilty to possessing firearms after being convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(9) and 924(a)(2). The district court sentenced Townsend to 46 months imprisonment and three years supervised release. Townsend appeals, arguing (1) a prior Iowa burglary conviction should not have been counted in calculating his criminal history points

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Ray, 411 F.3d 900 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) to Ray’s possession of firearms after his misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction. It held that the warning on his federal firearms license did not affirmatively misrepresent the law and therefore could not support an estoppel-by-entrapment defense.
excerpts: After Mr. Ray obtained his FFL, he was convicted in state court of misdemeanor domestic assault. Federal law prohibits a person who “has been convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence” from possessing a firearm. 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). When the Bureau of Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms got word that Mr. Ray had a number of firearms stored in his apartment, agents obtained and executed a search warrant and found seventy-two guns.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Borer, 412 F.3d 987 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court reviewed Borer’s conviction for possessing firearms while subject to domestic-violence protection orders, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8). The opinion applied the firearms prohibition in resolving his appeal and sentencing.
excerpts: Shane Borer pled guilty to possession of firearms while subject to one or more domestic-violence protection orders, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8). The firearms were discovered at Borer’s home on July 26, 2002, after a fire at his residence. At that time, Borer was subject to two protection orders.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Swartz v. Burger, 412 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court relied on its precedent applying 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), which prohibits firearm possession by a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence, in assessing the ex post facto challenge to Iowa’s analogous firearms restriction. It concluded that the state court’s decision was not an unreasonable application of clearly established law.
excerpts: Our own court reached largely the same conclusion with respect to an application of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), which prohibits possession of a firearm by a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. United States v. Pfeifer, 371 F.3d 430, 436-37 (8th Cir.2004).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Drapeau, 414 F.3d 869 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court applied the citizenship provision to hold that Indians granted U.S. citizenship are subject to the same legal restrictions as other American citizens. It further held that the citizenship statute reflected congressional intent to abrogate or modify contrary treaty provisions, including any purported treaty-based notice or delivery requirement.
excerpts: Finally, to the extent the treaty could be construed to impose a notice and request obligation on the United States, we have twice approved the opinion in United States v. Consolidated Wounded Knee Cases, 389 F.Supp. 235 (D.Neb.1975), which held that Congress’ grant of citizenship to the Indians, 8 U.S.C. § 1401(a)(2) (now § 1401(b), see Pub.L. No. 95-432, § 3, 92 Stat. 1046 (1978)), makes them “subject to all restrictions to which any other American citizen is subject, in any state,” and that the “legislative history and the language of the statute itself are sufficient expression of a clear Congressional intent to abrogate or modify any treaty provisions to the contrary.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Swipies v. Kofka, 419 F.3d 709 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court held that a noncustodial parent with court-ordered visitation possesses a protected liberty interest in participating in the care, custody, and management of the child. It further held that the alleged deprivation was not de minimis because the parent was scheduled to have visitation for two weeks.
excerpts: The due process clause of the fourteenth amendment says, in relevant part, that no state shall “deprive any person of ... liberty ... without due process of law.” U.S. Const, amend. XIV, § 1. To establish a procedural due process violation under this provision, a plaintiff must first show that the state infringed on a cognizable liberty interest.

If a state court affords a non-custodial parent visitation rights, we believe that the parent possesses, at least in some form, the liberty interest recognized in Manzano. A parent with visitation rights takes part in raising the child by making decisions about care, custody, and management during the period of the visitation, and thus he or she has the sort of parental role that deserves to be protected as a liberty interest.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Blair v. Wills, 420 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court applied the judge-made parental-rights principle that parents possess a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children and may direct their upbringing and education. Because Blair’s parents knowingly consented to his enrollment and delegated parental authority to school administrators, the court held that he could not maintain a false-imprisonment claim against the schools.
excerpts: Parents have a recognized liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children, Swipies v. Kofka, 348 F.3d 701, 703 (8th Cir.2003), and have the right to direct the upbringing and education of their children, Doe “A” v. Special School Dist. of St. Louis County, 637 F.Supp. 1138, 1146 (E.D.Mo.1986); Reece v. Reece, 890 S.W.2d 706, 710 (Mo.Ct.App.1995) (acknowledging that parent may arrange for another to provide care and education for minor child).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle, 427 F.3d 525 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court held that Rooker-Feldman did not bar federal jurisdiction because the requested prospective injunction would not interfere with a state-court judgment. It also applied Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process principles recognizing familial relations and held that Heartland had standing to assert a family-integrity claim based on its care and control of resident students.
excerpts: In the first appeal of this case, we rejected the challenge Waddle made to jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which prohibits federal-court review of a state-court judgment. We held that the injunctive relief Heartland was seeking would “not interfere with a state-court judgment”

We have recognized a right to familial relations, which includes the liberty interest of parents in the custody, care, and management of their children.” King v. Olmsted County, 117 F.3d 1065, 1067 (8th Cir.1997). And the Supreme Court held in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that a private school could assert such a claim on its own behalf.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Abdouch v. Burger, 426 F.3d 982 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court recognized that Melissa alleged deprivation of a liberty interest in the care and custody of her children, but affirmed qualified immunity for the defendants on that claim. The court also affirmed absolute immunity for the social workers’ initiation or maintenance of judicial termination proceedings.
excerpts: Melissa brought her claims in the present action under § 1983. She concedes that it initially was appropriate for the defendants to remove the children from her home. She alleges, however, that the defendants continued to seek the termination of her parental rights after it became clear that the defendants could not make the showing necessary to terminate her rights. She characterizes this action as a violation of her right to be free from prosecution without probable cause. She also alleges that the defendants’ protracted placement of C.A. in foster care deprived her of her liberty interest in the care and custody of her children. As to the prosecution-related claim, the district court found that the social workers were analogous to prosecutors and therefore entitled to absolute immunity for their initiation of judicial proceedings against Melissa. As to the alleged violation of her liberty interest as a parent, the district court found that qualified immunity applied. We affirm.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Dornheim v. Sholes, 430 F.3d 919 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court applied the substantive-due-process right of parents to control the care and custody of their children and balanced that interest against the State’s interest in protecting children. It held that officials conducting a child-abuse investigation are entitled to qualified immunity when their actions are reasonably founded on a suspicion of abuse, and that family integrity does not include a right to be free from child-abuse investigations.
excerpts: However, “[t]he right to family integrity clearly does not include a constitutional right to be free from child abuse investigations,” as the state has a strong interest in protecting the safety and welfare of minor children, particularly where protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves. Manzano v. S.D. Dep’t of Soc. Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 510 (8th Cir. 1995) (internal marks omitted).

These competing interests 'require us to balance the interests of the state and the children against the interests of the parent in determining whether a constitutional violation has occurred. “[W]hen a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.” Thomason v. SCAN Volunteer Servs., 85 F.3d 1365, 1371 (8th Cir.1996) (internal marks omitted).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Substantive Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Johnson v. University of Iowa, 431 F.3d 325 (8th Cir. 2005)
interps.summary: The court held that the parental liberty interest does not encompass a constitutional right to paid employer leave for bonding with a child. Because biological fathers are not a suspect class and paid parental leave is not a fundamental right, the University's distinction between adoptive and biological parents was subject to rational-basis review.
excerpts: Johnson contends that the policy should be reviewed with strict scrutiny because it interferes with his fundamental rights of child-rearing. Although the Supreme Court has recognized a number of fundamental rights concerning parents’ ability to raise their children, Johnson offers no precedent establishing that these rights include the ability to take time off from work to bond with a child. Furthermore, Johnson was allowed to take unpaid leave in accordance with the Family Medical Leave Act. He sued the University because he was unable to receive paid leave.

Because biological fathers are not a suspect class and because the right to paid leave is not fundamental, the appropriate standard of review is the rational basis test. Clayton v. White Hall Sch. Dist., 875 F.2d 676, 680 (8th Cir.1989) (upholding a school district’s policy of allowing the children of administrative employees, but not general employees, to open enroll into the district). A classification reviewed under this standard will be upheld “if it has some reasonable basis.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause and Equal Protection Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: K.D. ex rel. Deason v. County of Crow Wing, 434 F.3d 1051 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s substantive due process protection for parental custody and familial integrity. It held that an emergency removal of a child without a court order is constitutionally permissible when continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child’s health or welfare, and that the temporary removal here did not violate those rights.
excerpts: Parents have a liberty interest “in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Id. at 509. Parents and children have a constitutionally protected liberty interest in the care and companionship of each other. Whisman v. Rinehart, 119 F.3d 1303, 1309 (8th Cir.1997). However, “ ‘the liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling governmental interest in the protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.’ ” Manzano, 60 F.3d at 510 (quoting Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.1987)).

The circumstances under which a child can be removed from his or her parents’ custody without a court order are extremely limited. Deputy Galles removed K.D. from Deason’s custody under Minnesota Statutes § 260C.175, which provides that a child may be taken into immediate custody by a peace officer “when a child is found in surroundings or conditions which endanger the child’s health or welfare or which such peace officer reasonably believes will endanger the child’s health or welfare.” MinmStat. § 260C.175, subd. 1. In light of the facts discussed below, we conclude that Defendants did not violate Plaintiffs’ constitutional rights when K.D. was temporarily removed from Deason’s custody under this statute.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)
Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of children
Constitutionally protected familial integrity and parent-child companionship

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Olvey, 437 F.3d 804 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court held that the modified domestic-abuse protection order satisfied § 922(g)(8)(B) and (C)(ii) because it restrained Olvey from threatening, assaulting, molesting, attacking, or disturbing his wife’s peace. It also held that the post-order hearing satisfied § 922(g)(8)(A), making Olvey a prohibited person and supporting probable cause for the search warrant.
excerpts: Olvey’s argument centers on whether the warrant application demonstrated that he was a prohibited person under § 922(g)(8). The protection order as modified by the journal entry satisfies the requirements of § 922(g)(8)(B) and (C) because it restrains Olvey from threatening assaulting, molesting, attacking, or otherwise disturbing the peace of his wife. Furthermore, the journal entry “was issued after a hearing of which [Olvey] received actual notice, and at which [Olvey] had an opportunity to participate.” § 922(g)(8)(A).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Buster v. United States, 447 F.3d 1130 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) to determine whether the defendant’s prior domestic-abuse conviction involved a qualifying domestic relationship. It held that abuse perpetrated on a live-in girlfriend constitutes abuse committed by a person “similarly situated to a spouse.”
excerpts: We conclude Buster’s counsel was not ineffective and the district court did not err in dismissing Buster’s motion without an evidentiary hearing, because the undisputed facts underlying Buster’s prior conviction for domestic abuse could support a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g). Two of our sister circuits have addressed the issue before us, with one holding a “live-in girlfriend” qualifies as a domestic relationship for purposes of sections 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), and the other assuming as much.

We agree with the First and Fifth Circuits and hold abuse perpetrated on a live-in girlfriend is domestic abuse committed “by a person similarly situated to a spouse” for purposes of sections 922(g)(9) and 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). Cf. United States v. Cuervo, 354 F.3d 969, 998 (8th Cir.2004) (holding sufficient evidence supporte

norms.b_justification: Buster interpreted the phrase in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), “by a person similarly situated to a spouse.” That phrase appears verbatim in the current text, and the later amendments changed surrounding punctuation/conjunctions and added the dating-relationship category without altering the wording or function of the similarly-situated provision.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Porter ex rel. Pierce v. Knickrehm, 457 F.3d 794 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court rejected applying Rooker-Feldman to a federal challenge concerning the procedures governing an incapacitated person's admission and continued placement in a state human-development center, rather than a direct attack on the state guardianship judgment. It held that the confined person possessed a substantial liberty interest and evaluated the adequacy of the procedures under the Mathews framework and Parham.
excerpts: Porter filed his complaint alleging that the procedures governing admission and continuing placement were constitutionally infirm. The Officials filed a motion to dismiss. interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Citizens for Equal Protection v. Bruning, 455 F.3d 859 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court applied rational-basis equal-protection review to Nebraska’s definition of marriage as the union of one man and one woman. It held that the classification was entitled to a strong presumption of validity and assessed whether it was rationally related to legitimate state interests, including steering procreation into marriage.
excerpts: the classification created by § 29 and other laws defining marriage as the union between one man and one woman is afforded a “strong presumption of validity.” Heller v. Doe, 509 U.S. 312, 319, 113 S.Ct. 2637, 125 L.Ed.2d 257 (1993). The Equal Protection Clause “is not a license for courts to judge the wisdom, fairness, or logic of [the voters’] choices.

Our rational-basis review begins with an historical fact — the institution of marriage has always been, in our federal system, the predominant concern of state government. The Supreme Court long ago declared, and recently reaffirmed, that a State “has absolute right to prescribe the conditions upon which the marriage relation between its own citizens shall be created, and the causes for which it may be dissolved.” Pennoyer v. Neff, 95 U.S. 714, 734-35, 24 L.Ed. 565 (1878), quoted in Sosna v. Iowa, 419 U.S. 393, 404, 95 S.Ct. 553, 42 L.Ed.2d 532 (1975). This necessarily includes the power to classify those persons who may validly marry.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Gregg, 467 F.3d 1126 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court addressed Gregg’s conviction for possessing a firearm while subject to a restraining order, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8). The appeal concerned sentencing enhancements and acceptance of responsibility, rather than the validity or interpretation of the firearms prohibition.
excerpts: Bradley Gregg (Gregg) pled guilty to possessing a firearm while subject to a restraining order, in violation of 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(8) and 924(a)(2). The district court sentenced Gregg to 15 months’ imprisonment.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Estate of Korby v. Commissioner, 471 F.3d 848 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction rules to determine whether the decedent’s limited-partnership interest passed to the surviving spouse. It upheld the tax court’s treatment of the marital-deduction issue, including the estate’s concession that the deduction did not apply if only 38.26% of the partnership assets were included in the gross estate.
excerpts: Edna’s estate sought a marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2056, arguing Edna’s rights to and power over the KPLP assets passed to her husband at the time of her death under the terms of the living trust.

Ultimately, in resolving the marital deduction claim, Edna’s estate conceded the deduction did not apply if only 38.26% of the KPLP assets were included in Edna’s gross estate. Based upon that concession, the tax court included just 38.26% of KPLP’s assets when calculating the deficiency against Edna’s estate.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Ebrahim v. Gonzales, 471 F.3d 880 (8th Cir. 2006)
interps.summary: The court held that it lacked jurisdiction to review the denial of Ebrahim’s waiver request under 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(4). Whether the marriage was entered into in good faith was treated as a factual issue underlying the Attorney General’s discretionary waiver decision, which was not reviewable.
excerpts: Before reaching the merits of Ebrahim’s argument, however, we must first address the government’s argument that we are without jurisdiction to review petitions of the denial of a waiver under 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(4) because the question of whether a marriage has been entered into in “good faith” is a matter within the unre-viewable discretion of the Attorney General.

We recently held that we “lack jurisdiction to review questions of fact underlying discretionary decisions of the Attorney General, 8 U.S.C. §§ 1186a(c)(4), 1252(a)(2)(B), and are thus without jurisdiction to review the denial of the hardship waiver.... ” Suvorov v. Gonzales, 441 F.3d 618, 622 (8th Cir.2006).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(4)(A) and (B), concerning discretionary waivers and good-faith marriage determinations. Although later amendments changed agency references from the Attorney General to the Secretary of Homeland Security and added subsection (c)(4)(D), those changes did not alter the substance or function of subsections (c)(4)(A) and (B).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Thuy Thi Thanh Nguyen v. Mukasey, 522 F.3d 853 (8th Cir. 2008)
interps.summary: The court held that although the discretionary denial of a hardship waiver under 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(4)(B) is generally unreviewable, the court may review constitutional claims, questions of law, and nondiscretionary eligibility determinations underlying the waiver decision. The BIA had determined that Nguyen was not eligible even to be considered for a waiver because she failed to establish that her qualifying marriage was entered into in good faith.
excerpts: Although respondent is correct that we lack jurisdiction to review either the BIA’s discretionary decision to deny a hardship waiver, see 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii), or the BIA’s determinations, in relation to a hardship-waiver decision, as to what evidence is credible and how much weight to give that evidence, see 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(4)(B), we have jurisdiction to review constitutional claims or questions of law raised in a petition for review, see 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D), and we may also review the nondiscretionary determinations underlying the denial of relief

Here, the BIA did not exercise its discretion and deny Ms. Nguyen a waiver; rather, the BIA found that because Ms. Nguyen failed to prove that she entered into the qualifying marriage in good faith, she did not meet the eligibility requirements even to be considered for a hardship waiver.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(4)(B), governing the discretionary hardship waiver of the conditional-residence requirement. Later amendments changed agency terminology from “Attorney General” to “Secretary of Homeland Security” and added subsection (c)(4)(D), but did not substantively alter subsection (c)(4)(B)’s waiver standard or function.

requires the predicate misdemeanor have only one element: the use or attempted use of physical force (or its alternative, the threatened use of a deadly weapon ...).” Smith, 171 F.3d at 620.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Hassen v. Mukasey, 534 F.3d 927 (8th Cir. 2008)
interps.summary: The court applied the conditional-residence provisions governing adjustment to permanent-resident status based on marriage to a U.S. citizen. It held that adjustment must be denied when the marriage was entered into to obtain admission, and that the government bears the burden of proving a sham marriage by a preponderance of the evidence.
excerpts: Hassen argues that the IJ erred by not adjusting her conditional resident status to permanent resident status based on her marriage to a United States citizen. A person who is granted conditional resident status because of a marriage to a United States citizen can have that status adjusted to permanent resident upon proper request. 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c). Such an adjustment will be denied, however, if the marriage is found to have been entered into for the purpose of obtaining admission into the United States. ' 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(b) (1) (A) (i). The government bears the burden to prove by a preponderance of evidence that the marriage is a sham. 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(b)(2).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c), § 1186a(b)(1)(A)(i), and § 1186a(b)(2), concerning removal of conditional residence and the government’s preponderance-of-the-evidence burden to prove a marriage was entered into to procure admission. The post-decision amendments identified affected other provisions and did not substantively alter these interpreted rules, although the excerpt paraphrases rather than quotes the current statutory language verbatim.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Osakwe v. Mukasey, 534 F.3d 977 (8th Cir. 2008)
interps.summary: The court recognized that a prior determination of marriage fraud may permanently bar approval of a later immigrant visa petition, even if the alien subsequently enters a bona fide marriage with a U.S. citizen. Because the agency failed to reconcile conflicting determinations regarding the first marriage, the court remanded for further proceedings.
excerpts: Given the inconsistent rulings with respect to Osakwe’s first marriage, which the BIA failed to resolve, the propriety of its conclusion that Osakwe is statutorily ineligible for adjustment of status due to the CIS’s original determination of marriage fraud is called seriously into question. It goes without saying that the CIS’s determination of marriage fraud carries great consequences as an alien may be permanently ineligible to obtain an 1-130 visa even if he subsequently enters into a bona fide marriage with a U.S. citizen. See 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c) (“[N]o petition shall be approved if ... the Attorney General has determined that the alien has attempted or conspired to enter into a marriage for the purpose of evading the immigration laws.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c), which bars approval of a visa petition where the Attorney General has determined that the alien entered, attempted, or conspired to enter a marriage to evade the immigration laws. The listed post-2008 amendments affected other provisions and do not indicate any substantive change to subsection (c), although the supplied current-text excerpt does not reproduce that subsection verbatim.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Barzilay v. Barzilay, 536 F.3d 844 (8th Cir. 2008)
interps.summary: The court applied ICARA and the Hague Convention in holding that federal courts may adjudicate a Hague petition despite parallel state custody proceedings. Hague Convention article 16 requires custody proceedings to await resolution of the Hague litigation, and the pendency of state custody proceedings therefore does not justify Younger abstention.
excerpts: A party invokes the protections of the Convention in the United States by filing a petition in either federal or state court under ICARA (Hague petition). 42 U.S.C. § 11603(b) (“Any person seeking to initiate judicial proceedings under the Convention for the return of a child ... may do so by commencing a civil action by filing a petition for the relief sought in any court which has jurisdiction of such action and which is authorized to exercise its jurisdiction in the place where the child is located at the time the petition is filed.”); see § 11603(a) (vesting concurrent original jurisdiction over Hague petitions in the state and federal courts). ICARA further provides that “[t]he court in which an action is brought under [§ 11603(b)] shall decide the case in accordance with the Convention.” § 11603(d).

The Hague Convention requires that state court custody proceedings be stayed until the resolution of the Hague litigation. Hague Convention art. 16, T.I.A.S. No. 11670 (“[T]he judicial or administrative authorities of the Contracting State to which the child has been removed or in which it has been retained shall not decide on the merits of rights of custody until it has been determined that the child is not to be returned under this Convention.”) (emphasis added); Yang v. Tsui, 416 F.3d 199, 201 (3d Cir.2005). While ICARA does not have a similar express provision, the purpose of the Convention is to “provide for a reasoned determination of where jurisdiction over a custody dispute is properly placed.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Riehm v. Engelking, 538 F.3d 952 (8th Cir. 2008)
interps.summary: The court applied Rooker-Feldman but held that it did not bar the § 1983 Fourth Amendment claim because the plaintiffs had not participated in the ex parte state proceeding and did not seek to overturn the state order. The court also recognized the parental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of children, but rejected the familial-integrity claim because the detention did not violate the Fourth Amendment.
excerpts: We conclude that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine does not apply to David’s Fourth Amendment claim. First, the Riehms could not be considered parties to the ex parte petition. They had no opportunity to participate in the state court proceeding, either the CHIPS petition proceeding (prior to the February 28 hearing) or the ex parte petition proceeding in which the court issued the ex parte order. Second, the Riehms do not seek to overturn the ex parte order by this action. Rather, they seek redress under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for an alleged unconstitutional seizure of David.

Colleen also asserts a claim against Diercks regarding her Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in a familial relationship. "Our court has recognized the liberty interest which parents have in the care, custody, and management of their children.” Manzano v. S.D. Dep’t of Soc. Servs., 60 F.3d 505, 509 (8th Cir.1995). In Manzano, we granted a social worker qualified immunity because he investigated "upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.” Id. at 511. This case does not concern child abuse, but, as discussed above, Diercks had a "reasonable suspicion” of a threat to David’s welfare that justified the ex parte order removing David from his home. Because there was no Fourth Amendment violation surrounding David's detention, we reject Colleen’s claim.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Allen, 540 F.3d 821 (8th Cir. 2008)
interps.summary: The court upheld admission of a witness’s misdemeanor domestic-assault conviction to show that the witness himself was prohibited from possessing a firearm under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The conviction was relevant because it provided a motive for the witness to deny knowledge of or possession of the gun.
excerpts: The government offered his misdemeanor conviction to show Hall, Jr., himself, was prohibited from possessing a firearm. See 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). The district court properly perceived that, if Hall, Jr., admitted knowledge of or possession of the gun, he may have implicated himself in the commission of a crime. This provided a motive to disavow any knowledge of the firearm.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Sorenson v. Sorenson, 559 F.3d 871 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court held that Australia was the child’s habitual residence when the allegedly wrongful retention occurred. It therefore affirmed the district court’s ruling on Sorenson’s Article 15 Hague Convention claim.
excerpts: Eric Sorenson appeals the district court’s rulings on his claim under Article 15 of the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction (Hague Convention), 19 I.L.M. 1501 (1980), as implemented by the United States in the International Child Abduction Remedies Act, 42 U.S.C. § 11601-11610 (“ICARA”). Because we find that Australia was the child’s habitual residence at the time of the allegedly wrongful retention, we affirm the decision of the district court.

norms.b_justification: Sorenson interpreted Hague Convention Article 3’s habitual-residence requirement, as implemented by ICARA, through a fact-specific inquiry into the child’s circumstances and concluded that Australia was the habitual residence. That approach is functionally consistent with Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances formulation, although the record does not contain verbatim current-text language.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Hanggi v. Holder, 563 F.3d 378 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court rejected Hanggi’s claim that the BIA’s decision violated her constitutional right to due process in the context of her family-based immigration and removal proceedings. It therefore denied the petition for review.
excerpts: We also hold, assuming we have jurisdiction to do so, that the IJ did not abuse her discretion in denying the motion to terminate removal proceedings. Finally, we reject Hanggi’s suggestion that the BIA’s decision violated her constitutional right to due process. Accordingly, we deny the petition for review.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Ibrahimi v. Holder, 566 F.3d 758 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court applied the statutory and regulatory scheme governing conditional permanent residence based on marriage to a U.S. citizen. It held that an alien seeking a waiver of the joint-filing requirement must first establish that the qualifying marriage was entered into in good faith; only then does the Attorney General have discretion to grant the waiver and remove the conditions.
excerpts: Permanent-resident status conferred on the basis of a marriage to a U.S. citizen is granted initially on a conditional basis. Id. § 1186a(a)(l). Within ninety days prior to the two-year anniversary of the grant of conditional permanent-resident status, an alien can apply to have the conditional basis removed. Id. § 1186a(e)(3), (d)(2); 8 C.F.R. § 216.4(a)(1).

In order to establish eligibility for this good-faith marriage waiver or “hardship waiver,” the alien must first show that he or she entered into a “qualifying marriage ... in good faith.” Id. Only after the alien has established this fact does the Attorney General possess the discretion to grant the waiver and remove the conditional basis of the permanent-resident status. Id. If the Government denies the waiver application, the alien is entitled to seek review of the denial before the IJ during the course of removal proceedings. 8 C.F.R. § 216.5(f).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(a)(1), (c)(3), (d)(2), and (e)(3)–(4)(B), concerning conditional residence and the 90-day period for seeking removal of conditions. The 2011 amendment to § 1186a(a)(1) merely renumbered cross-references from subsections (g) to (h) after adding a new subsection (g), without changing the provision’s substantive function; the later amendments did not alter the interpreted requirements.

Ibrahimi interpreted 8 C.F.R. § 216.4(a)(1), particularly the requirement to file Form I-751 during the 90-day period before the second anniversary of conditional residence and the availability of a waiver when a joint petition cannot be filed. The current text preserves that timing requirement and waiver function; the cited excerpt is paraphrased rather than verbatim, so functional review is appropriate.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Parkhurst v. Tabor, 569 F.3d 861 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court held that a crime victim lacks a judicially cognizable equal-protection claim based solely on the state’s allegedly discriminatory failure to prosecute another person. Standing to challenge discriminatory prosecution is generally limited to persons who were prosecuted or threatened with prosecution.
excerpts: While it is well settled that defendants subjected to or threatened with discriminatory prosecution have standing to bring an equal protection claim, see Linda R.S., 410 U.S. at 619 & n. 5, 93 S.Ct. 1146, this right has not been extended to crime victims.

The Supreme Court concluded that Linda R.S. lacked standing to bring suit, explaining that “a citizen lacks standing to contest the policies of the prosecuting authority when he himself is neither prosecuted nor threatened with prosecution” because “a private citizen lacks a judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution or nonprosecution of another.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Equal Protection Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Abdelwahab v. Frazier, 578 F.3d 817 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court recognized and applied the statutory bar against granting an employment-based immigrant petition after a determination that the alien married to evade immigration laws. The court ultimately affirmed dismissal of the challenge to the petition revocation on jurisdictional, exhaustion, mootness, and remedial grounds.
excerpts: The Immigration and Nationality Act provides that no employment-based petition may be granted after a determination that an alien married "for the purpose of evading the immigration laws.” 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c), including the language barring approval of an employment-based petition after a determination that the alien married “for the purpose of evading the immigration laws.” That language remains verbatim and functionally unchanged; the listed later amendments affected other provisions, not subsection (c).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Yohannes v. Holder, 585 F.3d 402 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court applied the requirements for removing conditions on conditional permanent residence and construed the good-faith-marriage waiver under § 1186a(e)(4). It held that although the Attorney General’s ultimate waiver decision is discretionary, the court has jurisdiction to review the governing legal standard and whether the credited evidence satisfies it, while factual credibility determinations remain unreviewable.
excerpts: To remove the conditions on his status, Yohannes and Sharief were required to file a joint petition within ninety days of the two-year anniversary of the grant of conditional permanent residency and appear together at a personal interview. 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(3). Yohannes failed to satisfy this requirement.

Section 1186a(e)(4) provides that “[t]he determination of what evidence is credible and the weight to be given that evidence shall be within the sole discretion of the Attorney General.” In its motion to dismiss, the government argues that we cannot review the BIA’s denial of the waiver because 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(B)(ii) precludes our jurisdiction over decisions within the Attorney General’s discretion. Although the ultimate decision whether to grant the waiver is discretionary, we have jurisdiction to consider the legal standard for a good faith marriage and to determine whether the credited evidence meets that standard.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1186a(c)(3) and § 1186a(e)(4). Section (c)(3) was not substantively amended after the decision, and the later amendment affecting § (e)(4) merely replaced “Attorney General” with “Secretary of Homeland Security,” leaving the discretionary evidentiary standard unchanged in wording function.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Estate of Christiansen v. Commissioner, 586 F.3d 1061 (8th Cir. 2009)
interps.summary: The court applied the estate-tax marital-deduction rules under § 2056 and held that a dispute over the fair-market value of transferred assets did not make the transfer contingent or create a terminable interest. Valuation disputes concerning the date-of-death value therefore did not defeat the deduction.

As stated by the Tax Court below: That the estate and the IRS bickered about the value of the property being transferred doesn’t mean the transfer itself was contingent in the sense of dependent for its existence on a future event. It also recognized that procedural due process generally requires a hearing before deprivation of a protected family-related interest, absent extraordinary circumstances justifying postponement.

Robertson, 463 U.S. 248, 258, 103 S.Ct. 2985, 77 L.Ed.2d 614 (1983) (stating “the relationship of love and duty in a recognized family unit is an interest in liberty entitled to constitutional protection” under the Fourteenth Amendment);

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Lang v. Social Security Administration, 612 F.3d 960 (8th Cir. 2010)
interps.summary: The court held that 42 U.S.C. § 659 requires the United States to be treated like a private person in a state-court garnishment action enforcing child-support obligations. State procedural rules therefore governed service of the supplemental complaint, and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure did not apply merely because the garnishee was a federal agency.
excerpts: In order to facilitate the goal of the statute, the United States is treated the same as a private person would be treated for purposes of “legal process brought ... by an individual obligee, to enforce the legal obligation of the individual [i.e., a person entitled to moneys due from or payable by the United States] to provide child support or alimony.” 42 U.S.C. § 659(a).

In other words, whether government money due or payable to someone who owes child support will be subject to legal process must be “determined in accordance with State law in like manner as if the United States were a private person.” United States v. Morton, 467 U.S. 822, 831 n. 13, 104 S.Ct. 2769, 81 L.Ed.2d 680 (1984) (citations omitted). “Congress intended the Government to receive the same treatment as a private employer with respect to garnishment orders.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Amerson, 599 F.3d 854 (8th Cir. 2010)
interps.summary: The court applied the categorical approach to determine whether Amerson’s Nebraska misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction involved the use or attempted use of physical force under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). It held that the state plea-hearing factual recital, to which Amerson assented through counsel’s lack of objection, established the required force element and supported his § 922(g)(9) firearm conviction.
excerpts: Amerson contends that his Nebraska conviction did not involve the “use or attempted use of physical force.” See 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii). “Under the categorical approach, when a statute dictates that the predicate offense have enumerated elements, this court must ‘look only to the predicate offense rather than to the defendant’s underlying acts to determine whether the required elements are present.’ ” United States v. Howell, 531 F.3d 621, 622 (8th Cir.2008), quoting Smith, 171 F.3d at 620.

During Amerson’s plea hearing, the state judge adopted the factual recital that he and his girlfriend “got into an argument over the child and the defendant slapped her and pushed her head into the wall.” Amerson repeatedly states he did not “assent to” or “confirm” this factual basis. But his counsel stated he had “no objection” after the recital of facts. Thus, he assented to factual findings that satisfy the force requirement of 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii).

norms.b_justification: Amerson interpreted the physical-force requirement in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii), specifically the phrase “use or attempted use of physical force.” Although the 2022 amendment modified that clause by adding dating-relationship coverage and making a grammatical change, it did not alter the force requirement or its function, so the interpreted language remains substantively identical.
