The right to marriage is a substantive due process right, but actions that only collaterally effect family decisions do not violate the right to marry. Muir v. Decatur Cty., 917 F.3d 1050, 1053–54 (8th Cir. 2019).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Shawn Thomason, 991 F.3d 910 (8th Cir. 2021)
interps.summary: The court applied the federal interstate-stalking statute, 18 U.S.C. § 2261A(1), to Thomason’s prosecution. It rejected his argument that the statute impermissibly intruded on state police powers, explaining that Congress may regulate interstate commerce directly and that this prosecution did not regulate state governments.
excerpts: Fourth, Thomason argues that the interstate stalking statute, 18 U.S.C. § 2261A(1), is an unconstitutional “overreach of the federal legislature into a realm historically and exclusively controlled by the state police powers.” He does not challenge the authority of Congress to enact the provision under its power to regulate interstate commerce, but cites Printz v. United States, 521 U.S. 898, 923-24 (1997), for the proposition that the federal statute is “defective.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Justin Sholley-Gonzalez, 996 F.3d 887 (8th Cir. 2021)
interps.summary: The court held that § 922(g)(8) requires the protected person to be an intimate partner, but does not require the state protection order to expressly designate that person as an intimate partner. The order’s omission of that designation therefore did not prevent prosecution under § 922(g)(8) or violate due process notice requirements.
excerpts: An Iowa state court issued a protection order against Justin Dwight SholleyGonzalez. In issuing the order, the court did not expressly designate the protected person as an “intimate partner” under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), though the protected person was in fact an intimate partner. Under § 922(g)(8), a person subject to a court order protecting an intimate partner is restricted from possessing firearms and ammunition.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Chad Mink, 9 F.4th 590 (8th Cir. 2021)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit reviewed a jury instruction concerning the dangerous-weapon enhancement under 18 U.S.C. § 2261(b)(3). It held that, even assuming the instruction improperly removed the dangerous-weapon determination from the jury, Mink could not show prejudice because the enhancement would have applied regardless.
excerpts: Next, Mink contends that the district court erred by giving an instruction on Count 2 that presupposed that the vehicle (the red box truck) was a “dangerous weapon,” a finding necessary for an enhanced sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 2261(b)(3). The instruction for enhancement as to Count 2 stated: “[I]f you find the defendant guilty of the crime charged in that count, you will be asked in the verdict form to unanimously determine beyond a reasonable doubt whether the defendant used a dangerous weapon (a motor vehicle) during the commission of the offense.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Hal Stanley v. Asa Hutchinson, 12 F.4th 834 (8th Cir. 2021)
interps.summary: The court applied the parental liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of children, balancing it against the State’s compelling interest in protecting children. It held that officials removing children during an abuse investigation are protected by qualified immunity when the removal is founded on reasonable suspicion of child abuse, evaluated under the totality of the circumstances at the time of removal.
excerpts: Parents have a liberty interest in the care, custody, and management of their children,” but this interest is “limited by the state’s compelling interest in protecting a child . . . .” Swipies v. Kofka, 348 F.3d 701, 703 (8th Cir. 2003). To balance these competing interests, we have adopted the rule that, “when a state official pursuing a child abuse investigation takes an action which would otherwise unconstitutionally disrupt familial integrity, he or she is entitled to qualified immunity, if such action is properly founded upon a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.

Reasonable suspicion “must be determined by analyzing the totality of the circumstances at the time of the removal.” Stanley I, 899 F.3d at 629. “The liberty interest in familial relations is limited by the compelling government interest in protection of minor children, particularly in circumstances where the protection is considered necessary as against the parents themselves.” Myers v. Morris, 810 F.2d 1437, 1462 (8th Cir.), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 828 (1987).
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Simon Osagi Iyawe v. Merrick B. Garland, 28 F.4th 875 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The court applied 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c) to uphold denial of an I-130 petition because the noncitizen had previously sought immigration benefits through a marriage determined to be fraudulent. The court explained that the statutory bar is mandatory and applies even when the current marriage is bona fide or the prior conduct was not prosecuted.
excerpts: This rule is mandatory and bars approval of an I-130 petition if the noncitizen previously sought immigration benefits through a fraudulent marriage or attempted or conspired to do so, even if the current marriage is bona fide or if the noncitizen was never prosecuted for the past conduct. See Zerezghi v. U.S. Citizenship & Immigr. Servs., 955 F.3d 802, 804–05 (9th Cir. 2020) (citing Matter of Tawfik, 20 I. & N. Dec. 166, 167 (BIA 1990)).

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 U.S.C. § 1154(c), the mandatory bar on approving a visa petition when the beneficiary previously sought immigration benefits through a fraudulent marriage or attempted or conspired to do so. The post-decision amendment identified affects only § 1154(a)(1)(H), not subsection (c), so the interpreted language and function remain unchanged; the supplied current-text excerpt does not include subsection (c), preventing a text-identical determination.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Junior Roldan Marin, 31 F.4th 1049 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that sufficient evidence supported Roldan-Marin’s conviction under § 922(g)(8). The evidence showed that he knowingly possessed a firearm while subject to a no-contact order involving an intimate partner, and that the order remained in effect when he possessed the firearm.
excerpts: Viewed most favorably to the verdict, the evidence was sufficient to find that Roldan-Marin possessed a firearm with knowledge that he was subject to a nocontact order involving an intimate partner, in violation of § 922(g)(8). 2

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Flora Holmes v. Merrick B. Garland, 37 F.4th 520 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The court applied due-process principles in the family-immigration context and held that the immigration judge had not violated Holmes’s rights. The judge adequately explained the hearing’s purpose and Holmes’s rights and offered a continuance to obtain counsel.
excerpts: Judge Olmanson first found that Judge Nickerson had not violated Holmes’s due process rights because he had reviewed, in detail, the hearing’s purpose and Holmes’s rights and had asked Holmes if she wanted a continuance so that she could obtain an attorney.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Manda Roberson v. The Dakota Boys & Girls Ranch, 42 F.4th 924 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The court applied the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause to a child placed under state custody, holding that the state assumed a duty to provide adequate medical care after taking sole care, custody, and control of her. The state’s custody arrangement also established that the parents could not select treatment providers or remove the child from the facility.
excerpts: T]he Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause requires the State to provide involuntarily committed mental patients with such services as are necessary to ensure their reasonable safety from themselves and others.” (quotations omitted)); cf. Liebe v. Norton, 157 F.3d 574, 577 (8th Cir. 1998) (“[O]nce one is classified as a suicide risk, the right to be protected from that risk would seem to fall under the ambit of the right to have medical needs addressed.

When North Dakota took custody of A.A.R., it assumed the duty to give her adequate medical care. DJS had custody of A.A.R. As the Complaint alleges, “A.A.R. became a ward of the state of North Dakota in May of 2018 after numerous legal issues and a number of psychiatric hospitalizations,” and, “[a]s a result, . . . was placed at the [YCC].” The May 2018 Order effected these changes. The Order “removed [A.A.R.] from the care, custody and control of her parents,” and “placed [her] under the full care, custody and control of the State Department of Corrections, to be supervised by [DJS], . . . for a period of one year dating from May 3, 2018, or further order of the Court.
provisions: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1 (Due Process Clause)

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Andrew Redleaf v. CIR, 43 F.4th 825 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The court affirmed that Andrew’s deferred payments did not qualify as deductible alimony because the divorce instrument designated them as nondeductible and the payment obligation would have continued after Elizabeth’s death. Consequently, the payments were not taxable alimony income to Elizabeth and were treated as nontaxable transfers incident to divorce under § 1041.
excerpts: This dispute concerns deferred payments Andrew agreed to make to Elizabeth in 2012 and 2013. Andrew filed federal income tax returns claiming these were deductible “Alimony and separate maintenance payments” under 26 U.S.C. §§ 61(a)(8), 71(a)-(b), and 215(a). Elizabeth filed returns claiming the payments were nontaxable transfers of property incident to divorce. See 26 U.S.C. § 1041(a)(2), (c)(2).

Focusing on two of the four criteria that defined deductible alimony payments in § 71(b)(1), the Tax Court concluded (i) that Andrew’s obligation to make payments would have continued if Elizabeth had died before the final payment was due, 26 U.S.C. § 71(b)(1)(D); and (ii) that the MTA designated the payments as not includable in Elizabeth’s gross income and not deductible by Andrew, § 71(b)(1)(B).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Dennis Sryniawski, 48 F.4th 583 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The court construed § 2261A(2)(B) in a manner consistent with the First Amendment, holding that the statute requires intent to harass or intimidate and a course of electronic conduct causing, attempting to cause, or reasonably expected to cause substantial emotional distress. Under that interpretation, the evidence was insufficient to support Sryniawski’s cyberstalking conviction.
excerpts: A defendant is guilty of cyberstalking if he (1) “with the intent to . . . harass [or] intimidate,” (2) uses “any . . . electronic communication system of interstate commerce . . . to engage in a course of conduct,” that (3) “causes, attempts to cause, or would be reasonably expected to cause substantial emotional distress to” the victim or his immediate family. 18 U.S.C. § 2261A(2)(B).

The mens rea element, as charged in this case, requires that a defendant act with the intent to “harass” or “intimidate.” Id. § 2261A(2). If these terms are construed in their broadest sense, however, they would infringe on rights protected by the First Amendment. Broadly defined, “harass” can mean simply “to vex, trouble, or annoy continually or chronically.” Webster’s Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged 1031 (1993). “Intimidate” can mean “to make timid or fearful.” Webster’s Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged 1184 (2002).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Vladyslav Dubikovskyy v. Elena Goun, 54 F.4th 1042 (8th Cir. 2022)
interps.summary: The court applied the Hague Convention’s mature-child exception and ICARA’s corresponding burden of proof. The respondent had to prove by a preponderance that the child was sufficiently mature for the court to consider her views and that she objected to returning; when those requirements are met, the reasons for the objection are immaterial.
excerpts: For the mature child defense to apply, the respondent must establish by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) the child has attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of her views, and (2) the child objects to being returned. Custodio, 842 F.3d at 1089 (citing Hague Convention art. 13); see also 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e)(2)(B). If a child is found to be mature, the reasons the child objects to being returned are immaterial.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Lisa Crain v. Shirley Crain, 72 F.4th 269 (8th Cir. 2023)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit applied the domestic-relations exception and held that it did not bar federal diversity jurisdiction over a dispute involving marital-property distribution and interpretation of an agreement incorporated into a divorce decree. The court emphasized that the exception is narrow and applies only when the action’s subject is divorce, alimony, child support, or related marital-property distribution.
excerpts: We now turn to the domestic relations exception. This exception “‘divests the federal courts of jurisdiction over any action for which the subject is a divorce, allowance of alimony, or child support,’ including ‘the distribution of marital property.’” Wallace v. Wallace, 736 F.3d 764, 766 (8th Cir. 2013) (citation omitted). We have had limited occasion to analyze the domestic relations exception, but generally, we apply it only in narrow circumstances.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Christopher Cungtion, Jr., 72 F.4th 865 (8th Cir. 2023)
interps.summary: The court held that a violation of Iowa Code § 708.4, which requires an intent to cause harm to another person, necessarily involves the intentional use of physical force against another. Accordingly, the offense satisfies the force requirement for a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A)(ii) and supports the § 922(g)(9) firearms prohibition; Borden did not overrule the Eighth Circuit’s precedent.
excerpts: Iowa Code § 708.4. The fact that the statute requires an intent to cause harm to another person necessarily means that anyone who violates it has used “physical force against the person of another.”3 See Borden, 141 S. Ct. at 1826 (plurality opinion) (describing the “targeting” requirement of the force clause); id. at 1835 (Thomas, J., concurring in the judgment) (explaining why the “use of physical force” requires an “intentional act[] designed to cause harm”

We also reject the argument that the Supreme Court’s discussion in Borden of a federal domestic-violence statute, see 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(A), requires us to overrule Clark. See Borden, 141 S. Ct. at 1832–34. The problem with that statute is the missing “against[-]another” language, which does nothing to undermine our understanding of what qualifies as “bodily injury.” See Jima v. Barr, 942 F.3d 468, 472 (8th Cir. 2019); Rice, 813 F.3d at 705–06 & n.2.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Naoteru Tsuruta v. Sarah Tsuruta, 76 F.4th 1107 (8th Cir. 2023)
interps.summary: The court applied the Hague Convention’s wrongful-removal framework and held that Japan was the child’s habitual residence before removal. Habitual residence is determined by where the child was “at home” based on the totality of the circumstances, and does not require an actual parental agreement.
excerpts: The Hague Convention does not govern custody battles, instead the Hague Convention determines the proper forum for custody battles. Id. at 916–17. Under the Hague Convention, “a child wrongfully removed from her country of ‘habitual residence’ ordinarily must be returned to that country[]” where custody will be determined. Monasky v. Taglieri, 140 S. Ct. 719, 723 (2020).

A child’s habitual residence is “[t]he place where a child is at home, at the time of removal or retention[.]” Monasky, 140 S. Ct. at 726. An actual agreement between the parents is not required to establish habitual residence, instead “a child’s habitual residence depends on the totality of the circumstances specific to the case.” Monasky, 140 S. Ct. at 723.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Aarin Nygaard v. Tricia Taylor, 78 F.4th 995 (8th Cir. 2023)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit held that the Parental Kidnapping Prevention Act does not apply to Indian tribes because the statute requires the appropriate authorities of every “State” to enforce qualifying custody determinations and does not expressly include tribes. The court explained that the PKPA therefore did not require the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribal Court to recognize or enforce the North Dakota custody orders.
excerpts: The PKPA was enacted in 1980 to “facilitate the enforcement” of child custody orders across state lines and to “deter interstate abductions . . . of children undertaken” by parents “to obtain” a more favorable custody determination in another jurisdiction. Parental Kidnapping Prevention Act of 1980, Pub. L. No. 96-611, § 7(c), 94 Stat. 3566, 3569. The statute provides in relevant part that “[t]he appropriate authorities of every State shall enforce according to its terms . . . any custody determination . . . made consistently with the provisions of [the Act] by a court of another State.” 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(a).

A child custody order is “consistent with,” and therefore enforceable under, the PKPA if (1) the issuing state court “has jurisdiction” over the subject custody proceedings under state law and (2) one of five enumerated conditions is met. 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(c). The relevant condition in this case is that the “child’s home is or recently has been in the State.” Thompson, 484 U.S. at 177; see 28 U.S.C. § 1738A(c)(2)(A). Once a state court enters a custody determination “consistently with” the PKPA, that state’s jurisdiction over the subject custody proceedings “continues as long as . . . such State remains the residence of the child” or of any person, “including a parent or grandparent, who claims a right to custody” of the child.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Paul Essel v. Merrick Garland, 89 F.4th 686 (8th Cir. 2023)
interps.summary: The court treated the approved I-130 petition filed by Essel’s citizen spouse under the family-based immigration provisions as permitting Essel to seek adjustment of status, but emphasized that approval alone did not confer immigration status or guarantee eligibility. Because a final removal order was already in place, Essel needed to obtain reopening of the proceedings before pursuing adjustment.
excerpts: A United States citizen may file an I-130 petition with Immigration Services to request permanent resident status for an alien relative or spouse. See 8 U.S.C. § 1154(a)(1)(A)(i); 8 C.F.R. § 204.2(a)(1) (“A United States citizen or alien admitted for lawful permanent residence may file a [visa] petition on behalf of a spouse.

Though this approval did not itself grant any immigration status to Essel or guarantee his eligibility for a visa, it would normally allow him to apply for an adjustment of status. See 8 U.S.C. § 1255(a); Tebyasa v. Holder, 593 F.3d 707, 709 (8th Cir. 2010).
Because the Board already issued a final order of removal, Essel needed to file a motion to reopen with the Board to change his immigration status. See Tebyasa, 593 F.3d at 709; 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2.

norms.b_justification: The decision interpreted 8 C.F.R. § 204.2(a)(1), specifically the provision allowing a United States citizen or lawful permanent resident to file a petition on behalf of a spouse. That operative language remains substantively identical in the current text; the only discrepancy is the excerpt’s editorial “[visa]” insertion, while the 2025 amendment does not appear to alter this provision.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Jesse Sierra, 94 F.4th 721 (8th Cir. 2024)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 2261(a)(2) to Dustin Sierra’s conviction for aiding and abetting interstate domestic violence. It held that the evidence, viewed favorably to the verdict, was sufficient to show that he drove Jesse and E.W. from South Dakota into Nebraska or beyond the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation while a crime of violence was committed against E.W.
excerpts: Dustin challenges the sufficiency of the evidence for aiding and abetting interstate domestic violence by arguing there was no evidence that he took Jesse and E.W. to Nebraska or beyond the exterior boundaries of the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. Dustin was charged pursuant to 18 U.S.C. § 2261, which provides: A person who causes a spouse, intimate partner, or dating partner to travel in interstate or foreign commerce or to enter or leave Indian country by force, coercion, duress, or fraud, and who, in the course of, as a result of, or to facilitate such conduct or travel, commits or attempts to commit a crime of violence against that spouse, intimate partner, or dating partner, shall be punished as provided in subsection (b).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Eny Mejia Rodriguez v. Dennys Reyes Molina, 96 F.4th 1079 (8th Cir. 2024)
interps.summary: The court applied ICARA and Hague Convention article 13(b) in reviewing an order requiring the child’s return to Honduras. It held that the respondent had to prove by clear and convincing evidence that return would expose the child to a grave risk of physical or psychological harm or place her in an intolerable situation, and affirmed because that burden was not met.
excerpts: A child’s return is not required, for example, if the respondent establishes that “there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation.” Hague Convention art. 13b. The respondent must establish the existence of this narrow exception “by clear and convincing evidence,” 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e)(2)(A), meaning that he must show that a grave risk is “highly probable,” see Colorado v. New Mexico, 467 U.S. 310, 316 (1984).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Chad Mink, 107 F.4th 824 (8th Cir. 2024)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 2261(a)(1) in rejecting Mink’s argument that attempted predicate offenses could not qualify as crimes of violence. It explained that § 2261(a)(1) expressly criminalizes an attempt to commit a crime of violence, making Borden and Taylor inapposite to his interstate-domestic-violence convictions.
excerpts: Mink relies on these cases to challenge the validity of his convictions on counts 3 and 10 of the indictment for interstate domestic violence, an element of which requires that the defendant commit or attempt to commit a crime of violence against an intimate partner. See 18 U.S.C. § 2261(a)(1). He argues that the uncharged predicate offenses specified in the jury instructions—attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, attempted arson, attempted willful injury, and attempted assault with a dangerous weapon—do not qualify as crimes of violence under § 2261(a)(1) because these offenses do not require as an element “the use, attempted use, or threatened use of force.

value, given that § 2261(a)(1) explicitly criminalizes an attempt to commit a crime of violence, whereas the force clauses at issue in Borden and Taylor do not, see Taylor, 596 U.S. at 853, it follows that these cases did not effect a sea change relating to a conviction for interstate domestic violence. Mink cites no authority indicating otherwise.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Frank Bibeau v. CIR, 108 F.4th 1038 (8th Cir. 2024)
interps.summary: The court held that the Indian Citizenship Act made all native-born Indians United States citizens and that citizenship subjects them to federal taxation absent a specific statutory or treaty exemption. It further held that the Act’s tribal-property proviso does not create a tax exemption.
excerpts: Since the Act took effect in 1924, all native-born Indians have been citizens of the United States, 8 U.S.C. § 1401(b), and the Internal Revenue Code does not grant tax exemptions solely because someone is an Indian—a suggestion Supreme Court precedent clearly precludes.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Devon Arseneau v. Elaine Pudlowski, 110 F.4th 1114 (8th Cir. 2024)
interps.summary: The court applied Younger abstention’s three-part framework to the family-custody dispute. It held that abstention was unwarranted because no state-court proceedings concerning the subject of the federal suit were ongoing, so the first Younger requirement was not satisfied.
excerpts: Younger abstention requires that federal courts “abstain from exercising their jurisdiction if (1) there is an ongoing state proceeding, (2) that implicates important state interests, and (3) that provides an adequate opportunity to raise any relevant federal questions.” Tony Alamo Christian Ministries v. Selig, 664 F.3d 1245, 1249 (8th Cir. 2012). There are no ongoing state court proceedings pertaining to the subject of this suit. Thus, the first component of Younger abstention is not met.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Lester Brown, 122 F.4th 290 (8th Cir. 2024)
interps.summary: The court applied the cyberstalking statute and held that sufficient evidence supported Brown’s conviction for cyberstalking resulting in death. The evidence permitted the jury to find the required intent, interstate electronic communications, resulting fear or substantial emotional distress, and Harris’s death resulting from the stalking.
excerpts: To prove Brown guilty of cyberstalking resulting in death, the Government had to show that Brown, (i) “with the intent to kill, injure, harass, intimidate, or place under surveillance with intent to kill, injure, harass, or intimidate another person,” (ii) “use[d] the mail, any interactive computer service or electronic communication service or electronic communication system of interstate commerce, or any other facility of interstate or foreign commerce to engage in a course of conduct that” (iii) “place[d] that person in reasonable fear of . . . death . . . or serious bodily injury,” or “cause[d], attempt[ed] to cause, or would be reasonably expected to cause substantial emotion distress to [that] person,” and (iv) that the person died as a result. 18 U.S.C. §§ 2261A(2), 2261(b)(1). We conclude that a jury could reasonably conclude that all four elements were met.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Michael Hoeft, 128 F.4th 917 (8th Cir. 2025)
interps.summary: The court addressed the constitutionality of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), which prohibits firearm possession by persons convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence. It declined to decide the constitutional issue because any error in retaining that charge was harmless: the jury separately found Hoeft guilty under § 922(g)(1) and § 922(g)(9).
excerpts: We pass no judgment here on § 922(g)(9), which prohibits people convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence from possessing guns. Any error in refusing to dismiss that portion of the charge was harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. The jury stated in a special verdict form that it found Hoeft guilty under both § 922(g)(1) and (g)(9), so it would have convicted Hoeft on the gun charge even if § 922(g)(9) was removed from the indictment.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Donglan Xia v. Kika Scott, 129 F.4th 1084 (8th Cir. 2025)
interps.summary: The court applied 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1)(E) to Xia’s petition seeking immediate-relative classification for her adopted nephew. It also relied on Hague Adoption Convention Article 14’s habitual-residence framework in evaluating whether the adoption fell outside the Convention, and remanded because the agency’s analysis was erroneous.
excerpts: As a United States citizen, in January 2018, Xia filed an I-130 petition to classify Tim as an immediate relative to get preferential immigration status for him. See 8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1)(E) (2023). Because China is a party to the Hague Adoption Convention, classification under an I-130 petition was available for Tim only if his adoption was not subject to the Convention.

Xia could have demonstrated Tim’s adoption fell outside the Hague Adoption Convention by submitting evidence showing he was habitually resident in the United States at the time of his adoption. See 32 I.L.M. 1135, Hague Adoption Convention, Art. 14.

According to USCIS’s guidance, a United States citizen petitioner who is habitually resident in the United States may prove that the “Hague Adoption Convention does not apply” by showing that her “child is not habitually resident in” another Hague Adoption Convention country.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Jae Bernard, 136 F.4th 762 (8th Cir. 2025)
interps.summary: The Eighth Circuit affirmed Bernard’s conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), rejecting his facial Second Amendment challenge. The court held that the statute is not facially unconstitutional because a facial challenge requires showing that no valid application exists.
excerpts: Jae Michael Bernard appeals his conviction for unlawful possession of a firearm by a person convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence. See 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9). Bernard moved to dismiss the indictment on the ground that § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutional on its face under the Second Amendment. The district court* denied the motion, and we affirm.

Bernard argued that § 922(g)(9) is unconstitutional on its face because there is no historical tradition supporting a categorical, lifetime ban on the possession of firearms by persons convicted of a misdemeanor offense. The district court denied the motion, and Bernard entered a conditional guilty plea, reserving his right to appeal the denial of his motion to dismiss.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: United States v. Principal Springer, 141 F.4th 947 (8th Cir. 2025)
interps.summary: The court held that Springer’s as-applied Second Amendment challenge to 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9) could not affect his conviction because the indictment charged an alternative § 922(g)(3) basis that independently made his firearm possession unlawful. The court therefore affirmed the conviction without deciding whether § 922(g)(9) itself is constitutional.
excerpts: It also ends his as-applied challenge to the domestic-abuser-in-possession statute, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(9), but for a different reason. A “conviction can be sustained on any one of the § 922(g) categories” because just one is enough to make the possession illegal. United States v. Marin, 31 F.4th 1049, 1054 n.2 (8th Cir. 2022).

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Philip Myers v. Pamela Bondi, No. 23-3286 (8th Cir. 2025)
interps.summary: The court applied the derivative-citizenship requirements in 8 U.S.C. § 1431, including the requirement that an adopted child satisfy the adopted-child definition in § 1101(b)(1)(E)(i). It held that the two-year legal-custody and residence requirement was not unconstitutional as applied to Myers, despite his alleged abuse by the adoptive parent.
excerpts: The provisions of § 1431(a), however, apply to a “child” adopted by a United States citizen parent only in specified circumstances—i.e., “if the child satisfies the requirements applicable to adopted children under [8 U.S.C. § 1101(b)(1)].” 8 U.S.C. § 1431(b) (2004). As of 2004, when Myers’s adoptive mother became a naturalized citizen, § 1101(b)(1) defined “child” to include “a child adopted while under the age of sixteen years if the child has been in the legal custody of, and resided with, the adopting parent or parents for at least two years.” Id. § 1101(b)(1)(E)(i) (emphasis added).

The Constitution vests Congress with the “Power . . . [t]o establish an uniform Rule of Naturalization,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 4, and the “scope of judicial inquiry into immigration legislation” is “limited.” Fiallo v. Bell, 430 U.S. 787, 792 (1977). The 2004 version of § 1101(b)(1)(E)(i) reflects a legislative policy decision to distinguish between adopted children who have lived in the custody of their adopting parents for at least two years and those who have not, without inquiry into the conditions of life in the home.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Abrahim Fofana v. Kristi Noem, No. 24-2485 (8th Cir. 2026)
interps.summary: The court construed the filing right and exception in 8 U.S.C. § 1154(a)(1)(A), explaining that Bremer involved whether those provisions applied to the filing at all. interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Lucas Alzu v. Amy Huff, No. 24-2517 (8th Cir. 2026)
interps.summary: The court applied ICARA and Hague Convention principles governing wrongful removal, holding that the petitioner bears the burden of proving wrongful removal or retention. Applying Monasky’s totality-of-the-circumstances, fact-driven standard, the court affirmed the finding that Argentina was not the child’s habitual residence.
excerpts: The determination of a child’s habitual residence is a mixed question of law and fact. Monasky, 589 U.S. at 84. “Once the trial court correctly identifies the governing totality-of-the-circumstances standard, . . . [t]he habitual residence determination . . . should be judged on appeal by a clear-error review standard deferential to the factfinding court.” Id.; See also Tsuruta v. Tsuruta, 76 F.4th 1107, 1111 (8th Cir. 2023) (same).
The petitioner bears the burden of proving ‘that the child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of the Convention.’” Id. at 917, citing 42 U.S.C. § 11603(e)(1)(A).
L]ocating a child’s home is a fact-driven inquiry[.] [C]ourts must be ‘sensitive to the unique circumstances of the case and informed by common sense.

interps.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
interps.citation: Michael Cunningham v. Eric Olson, No. 24-3261 (8th Cir. 2026)
interps.summary: The court applied 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii) in determining the effect of Missouri’s expungement statute on a person’s federal firearm-possession rights. It held that the expungement order restored Cunningham’s right to possess a firearm under federal law.
excerpts: The expungement statute’s text further reinforces this conclusion. In 2022, at the time of Cunningham’s arrest, the statute explicitly provided that expungement orders would restore the right to possess a firearm under federal law. § 610.140.8 (effective Aug. 28, 2021) (citing 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(33)(B)(ii)).
